papers.title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
papers.abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08298 .
papers.summary: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address.

papers.title: Redeploying the Jockeys: The Intermediary Role of Venture Capital in Entrepreneurial Labor Markets
papers.abstract: This paper explores how venture capitalists (VCs) add value by examining their role as labor market intermediaries. Using novel data, I show that VCs create internal labor markets (ILMs) to facilitate entrepreneurial mobility across their portfolio firms. Survey evidence suggests that VCs leverage private information about founders’ abilities to strategically match talent to portfolio firms, creating value for the recipient companies. Consistent with this mechanism of asymmetric learning, I find that (a) former VC partners continue to influence founder mobility, (b) ILM intensity positively predicts VC fund returns, and (c) the ILM effect is stronger when information asymmetry is greater. This paper was accepted by Lin William Cong, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.01626 .
papers.summary: This paper explores how venture capitalists (VCs) add value by examining their role as labor market intermediaries. Using novel data, I show that VCs create internal labor markets (ILMs) to facilitate entrepreneurial mobility across their portfolio firms.

papers.title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
papers.abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the construction of a new measure of human-perceived difficulty rating for each knapsack instance, we found evidence that players who were assigned to instances with a higher difficulty rating in the past tended to perform better on future attempts. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: S. papers.summary: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others.

papers.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
papers.abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09021 .
papers.summary: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations.

papers.title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
papers.abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: K. J. Mitchener thanks the Ciocca Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation at Santa Clara University for funding this research (Grant 2024-CIOG11). Any views expressed in this paper exclusively represent those of the authors and do not reflect the official viewpoint of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, the European Central Bank, or the Eurosystem. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03635 .
papers.summary: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work?

papers.title: Recommender Systems Under Privacy Protection
papers.abstract: We examine how a profit-driven platform designs its recommender policies under varying privacy protection regimes. We demonstrate a functional equivalence between opt-out protection and unprotected privacy. Notably, granting consumers the autonomy to misrepresent personal data can compel the platform to distort recommendations, inadvertently harming both parties. When recommendations are purely informative, such privacy controls can deter personalization entirely. However, when recommendations also serve an allocative role—controlling product access—algorithmic discrimination may emerge, restricting the disadvantaged minority from valuable opportunities. These findings remain robust even with endogenous profit margins. This paper was accepted by Omar Besbes, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05007 .
papers.summary: We examine how a profit-driven platform designs its recommender policies under varying privacy protection regimes. We demonstrate a functional equivalence between opt-out protection and unprotected privacy.

papers.title: Uncertainty Attitudes, Subjective Beliefs, and Decisions Under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: We conducted survey experiments to gather new data on uncertainty attitudes and subjective beliefs. Our survey targets a general population, focusing on health and financial decisions. We collect data on (i) individual attitudes toward risk and ambiguity, including individual-specific probability weighting and loss aversion, and (ii) individual probabilistic beliefs about events related to the decisions we consider. The joint availability of individual preference parameters and subjective beliefs allows us to study heterogeneity and cross-correlations across these parameters in depth and to estimate structural models of decision making under uncertainty that go beyond subjective expected utility. We find that both preferences and beliefs are highly heterogeneous. Compared with subjective expected utility, prospect theory combined with source-dependent probability weighting fits the data strictly better in some contexts and equally well in others. Prospect theory performs particularly well when the belief distribution is concentrated toward extreme values. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: A. Delavande acknowledges funding from the Economic and Social Research Council Research Centre on Micro-Social Change [Grants ES/L009153/1 and ES/S012486/1] and the National Institute on Aging [Grant P01AG008291]. J. Ganguli acknowledges research support from the Economic and Social Research Council [Grant ES/K00168X/1]. F. Mengel acknowledges support from the European Research Council [Grant DYNNET-805017]. Ethical approval was obtained by the Ethics Social Sciences subcommittee at the University of Essex in August 2015. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06232 .
papers.summary: We conducted survey experiments to gather new data on uncertainty attitudes and subjective beliefs. Our survey targets a general population, focusing on health and financial decisions.

papers.title: Incumbents’ Alliances and (Non-)Adaptation During the Pre-Commercialization Stage of a New Technology
papers.abstract: Research on incumbent adaptation through alliances typically assumes that incumbents can entice partners to share proprietary knowledge in a new technology by offering access to valuable complementary assets. This assumption fits the commercialization stage of a new technology, when both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets hold high value. However, during the pre-commercialization stage—when proprietary knowledge in the new technology is valuable but incumbents’ complementary assets cannot yet be fully deployed to commercialize the new technology—this logic may not hold. We develop a framework that explains how stage-dependent shifts in the value of both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets alter the bargaining power between incumbents and knowledge-possessing firms, thereby reshaping the adaptive potential of alliances. Using data on the semiconductor industry during the emergence of nanotechnology, we found that alliances between semiconductor incumbents and nanotechnology-capable partners are less likely to form and, even when formed, are less likely to focus on the explicit transfer of proprietary knowledge in emerging nanotechnology. Moreover, these alliances are more likely to be structured as joint ventures, especially when the risk of knowledge leakage is heightened. Joint venture arrangements, in turn, impede semiconductor incumbents’ post-alliance nanotechnology invention more than contractual arrangements. Taken together, we develop insights into how incumbents may struggle to use alliances for adaptive learning during the pre-commercialization phase of a new technology.
papers.summary: Research on incumbent adaptation through alliances typically assumes that incumbents can entice partners to share proprietary knowledge in a new technology by offering access to valuable complementary assets.

papers.title: Interface as a design choice: How the implementation of interfaces influences coordination and performance in modular systems
papers.abstract: Research Summary Modular systems play a central role in technological innovation. Such systems emerge when interdependencies among modules in a complex system are isolated through interfaces. While early seminal work highlighted the importance of interface design, subsequent research on modularity has largely overlooked it. We develop a model that treats interfaces as a set of design choices, separate from module choices. This model elucidates the mechanisms through which interface design influences system performance and identifies novel strategies for sequencing the search of interface and module designers to improve outcomes. The framework has implications not only for standalone innovations but also for the design of standards in platforms and ecosystems. Ultimately, it demonstrates that interface design is as much a strategic challenge as it is a technical one. Managerial Summary Managers increasingly rely on modular designs to enable innovation, yet often overlook interfaces as a strategic lever. This study shows that actively designed and periodically updated interfaces can coordinate interdependencies without constraining decentralized search, enabling modular systems to approach the performance of integrated designs. Crucially, sequencing matters: allowing modules to evolve before introducing interfaces improves long‐run performance, as early experimentation generates knowledge that interfaces can later build upon. Finally, infrequent interface redesign is sufficient to sustain coordination, reducing the need for continuous adaptations. Overall, interfaces should be treated as evolving strategic choices that shape innovation trajectories in products, platforms, and ecosystems.
papers.summary: Research Summary Modular systems play a central role in technological innovation. Such systems emerge when interdependencies among modules in a complex system are isolated through interfaces.

papers.title: Growth Paths in Early Machine Learning Ventures: Technical Configuration and Competitive Advantage Over Time
papers.abstract: Machine learning capabilities have become important strategic assets, yet little is known about how their technical characteristics affect the competitive advantage of the firms that build them. Through an inductive, multicase study tracking six early-stage machine learning ventures in an accelerator program, we explore how their phases of specialization and exploration may be constrained by properties of the underlying technology. Our findings show how training data, learning paradigms, and model outputs depend on one another and on the applications they serve, and how these relationships change over time. This interdependence shapes firms’ growth paths, alternately expanding or limiting the strategic options available to them. Characteristics that confer an early competitive advantage can constrain later growth. We discuss the implications for strategy research on competitive advantage and path dependence in machine learning ventures.
papers.summary: Machine learning capabilities have become important strategic assets, yet little is known about how their technical characteristics affect the competitive advantage of the firms that build them.

papers.title: Knowledge protection and modularity of innovation activities in firms: Evidence from US trade secrecy law
papers.abstract: Research Summary Strategy scholars have theoretically explored the relationship between legal knowledge protection and modularity of innovation activities in firms, but this relationship has yet to be empirically tested in the literature. Leveraging state‐level changes in US trade secrecy law and using a network modularity measure, this paper examines how trade secret protection affects the modularity of firms' innovation activities. Analyzing intrafirm inventor collaboration patterns in US patent data from 783 high‐tech firms between 1976 and 2017, we find that increased trade secret protection is negatively associated with the modularity of innovation activities within firms. This effect is more pronounced for firms with superior technologies and those geographically collocated with competitors—factors that enhance firms' knowledge appropriability concerns—and less pronounced for firms in industries where alternative appropriability mechanisms are highly effective. Moreover, our findings suggest that the increased betweenness centrality of new hires (skilled and junior) serves as an important underlying mechanism for the treatment effect. These results contribute to the literature by illuminating how firms strategize their internal innovation activities for knowledge protection and by underscoring its underlying mechanism. This study demonstrates that stronger legal mechanisms alleviating firms' knowledge protection concerns, such as increased trade secret protection, encourage firms to adopt a less modularized, more integrated innovation system. papers.title: The Impact of Commercial Real Estate Regulations on U.S. Output
papers.abstract: Commercial real estate accounts for about 20% of the U.S. capital stock and is highly regulated. Yet relatively little is known about how these regulations affect economic activity or consumer welfare. This paper develops a spatial general equilibrium model of the U.S. economy with commercial real estate regulations and congestion effects, the latter providing a rationale for such regulations. The model constructs a panel of commercial real estate regulation indices for major U.S. metropolitan areas by exploiting variation in the share of parcel value attributable to land versus structures in tax assessor records compiled by Cotality. We find that a moderate relaxation of commercial real estate building regulations across U.S. cities generates large allocative efficiency gains, increasing output by 2.7% to 5.3% and welfare by 2.8% to 8.0% of lifetime consumption. We then extract the component of our regulatory indices that covaries with specific zoning attributes in LightBox data, including zoning height limits, and use it to simulate local deregulation policies. Relaxing height limits in New York City raises its output by 2.9%.
papers.summary: Commercial real estate accounts for about 20% of the U.S. capital stock and is highly regulated. Yet relatively little is known about how these regulations affect economic activity or consumer welfare.

papers.title: Deregulation, Market Structure, and the Evolution of U.S. Banking
papers.abstract: We construct novel network-based measures of U.S. state-level bank deregulation intensity that allow us to separately identify the effects of deregulation on competition and investment opportunities. In contrast to existing studies, we find that increased competition leads to higher deposit funding costs and a reduction in banks’ net interest margins and profitability. In response, banks shift their business models and persistently increase their risk taking. Our findings resolve conflicting evidence in the literature and support theories in which reductions in bank charter values lead to higher bank risk taking. This paper was accepted by Camelia Kuhnen, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01128 .
papers.summary: We construct novel network-based measures of U.S. state-level bank deregulation intensity that allow us to separately identify the effects of deregulation on competition and investment opportunities.

papers.title: A platform for change? Core component innovations, complementor adaptation, and multihoming in platform‐based ecosystems
papers.abstract: Research Summary Digital platforms coordinate complementor innovations through interfaces into their core components. However, when interfaces themselves evolve alongside core component innovations, complementors may exhibit behaviors that are not entirely predictable. Using granular data from Apple's five major iOS releases, we abductively examine App developers’ responses following Apple's core component innovations. We document that, in post‐release periods, complementors simultaneously increase co‐innovation on iOS while being more likely to multihome by diversifying to the competing platform. These choices are further explained by whether architectural changes reflect cross‐platform standardization or platform‐specific differentiation. Standardization spurs both complementor co‐innovation and multihoming, while differentiation reduces diversification tendencies. The patterns that we document reveal an important tension: governing through interfaces enables platforms’ scalability but constrains their ability to control complementors as platforms evolve. Managerial Summary Digital platforms like Apple coordinate large scale innovation through standardized interfaces, but those interfaces must evolve as platforms compete, and the direction of that evolution has consequences managers should attend to. Analyzing Apple's five major iOS releases, we find that architectural changes are associated with increased co‐innovation but also a higher likelihood that developers diversify to a competing platform. This pattern is particularly pronounced when updates bring iOS closer to Android, suggesting that architectural convergence may lower the barriers to cross‐platform expansion for developers. Importantly, this behavior is strongest among highest‐value developers. papers.title: When money isn't everything: Identifying stage‐based patterns of entrepreneurial resource acquisition
papers.abstract: Research Summary Scholars often examine how entrepreneurs' existing ties predict resource acquisition. We investigated the reverse: How does the act of pitching generate new ties with investors? Using the context of the Slow Money community, we analyzed social entrepreneurs' pitches to impact investors. Rather than identify a single strategy that benefited all firms, we found that “stage‐appropriate framing” facilitated resource acquisition by aligning with investors' expectations. Late‐stage entrepreneurs who emphasized financial process framing acquired more financial capital. Conversely, early‐stage entrepreneurs who emphasized social process framing developed more investor ties. By shifting attention from the importance of pre‐existing networks to the potential of entrepreneurial pitches, our research explains how pitch framing can facilitate the acquisition of both financial capital and investor ties, thereby mitigating liabilities for early‐stage firms. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs know that pitches help raise money, but we discovered that they also foster investor ties. In studying pitch competitions in the Slow Money community, we found that different messages resonated with investors depending on a firm's stage. Early‐stage entrepreneurs gained more investor ties when their pitches highlighted a willingness to collaborate and engage in true partnerships. Late‐stage entrepreneurs attracted more funds when they focused on their business track record. In both cases, matching the pitch framing to the firm stage—and using engaging behavioral cues—helped founders attract stage‐appropriate resources. Our research shows that entrepreneurs can raise not just financial capital but also build investor ties without relying on pre‐existing networks—when their pitch aligns with their stage.
papers.summary: Research Summary Scholars often examine how entrepreneurs' existing ties predict resource acquisition. We investigated the reverse: How does the act of pitching generate new ties with investors?

papers.title: Signaling in Repeated Delegation
Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
papers.abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Consistent with diagnostic expectation theory, higher exposure to Ebola fear does not result in a significant learning effect during the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal acknowledges the financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. Y. Lin gratefully acknowledges financial support from the NUS Research Grant [Grants A-8001725 and A-8004426]. R. Lu and X. Zhang acknowledge the financial support of the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 71903005, 72402005, and 72472001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01919 .
papers.summary: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation.

papers.title: Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
papers.abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In all cases, the whiplash effect persists, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our findings. Finally, we use our theory model prediction as a feature and apply machine learning techniques to predict the time that vessels spend in Shanghai Port after a typhoon disruption and show that using our model predictor, alongside all relevant vessel and voyage attributes as raw features, significantly reduces prediction errors by 10%–30% on average compared with not using it. papers.title: Advertising by Recruiting Influencers
papers.abstract: The rise of social media platforms has enabled customers to rely on influencers and peer reviews to guide their purchasing decisions. As products increasingly focus on experiences, firms are leveraging influencer marketing as a crucial tool. This paper addresses key challenges of influencer marketing by considering different types of influencers and partnership schemes alongside the impact of social learning. We introduce a two-period model wherein, in the initial period, the firm unveils a new product experience of unknown quality alongside an influencer marketing campaign. The campaign relies on two types of influencers that differ in popularity and engagement levels and two partnerships: sponsored advertising and public relations. Customers base their purchasing decisions on their original (heterogeneous) beliefs, influencer-driven information, and reviews from early adopters in the second period. When customers are equally likely to follow any given influencer, the firm should choose a single influencer type and partnership. Consumer reviews complement influencer marketing when products are initially undervalued, increasing the returns to influencer investment. Moreover, within a societal structure characterized by distinct classes, in which followers and influencers often belong to the same class, a mix of influencer types and partnership schemes may become optimal. Our study provides guidance on selecting influencer types, partnership schemes, and social media platforms based on engagement, popularity, audience composition, and platform characteristics. This paper was accepted by Jeanette Song, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07919 .
papers.summary: The rise of social media platforms has enabled customers to rely on influencers and peer reviews to guide their purchasing decisions. As products increasingly focus on experiences, firms are leveraging influencer marketing as a crucial tool.

papers.title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
papers.abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .
papers.summary: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021.

papers.title: Drifting to the top? The effects of category erraticism on status mobility in the U.S. venture capital industry
papers.abstract: Research Summary We examine the effects of category erraticism, that is, having moved across socio‐cognitively distant industry categories over time, on status mobility. We argue that it is not the breadth of the categories that a firm spans or the overall distance among those categories, but whether its movement across categories forms a coherent or incoherent trajectory, that hinders upward status mobility by creating commitment and capability concerns among external audiences. We further argue that these concerns are more problematic for higher status firms and more experienced firms because they are subjected to stricter expectations of trajectory coherence. Using a comprehensive longitudinal sample of 1413 venture capital firms (VCs) in the U.S. VC industry from 1980 to 2012, we find that category erraticism reduces upward status mobility. This effect is partly mediated by the extent to which external audiences are concerned about the commitment and capability of the VCs, and is stronger for higher‐status and more experienced VCs. Managerial Summary This study shows that how venture capital firms (VCs) move across industries over time shapes their status position in the VC industry. VCs that move across distant sectors in ways that appear incoherent, often described in the industry as thesis drift, strategy drift, or tourist VC behavior, raise concerns about their long‐term commitment and ability to add value to the firms in which they invest. These concerns make it harder for such firms to form syndication relationships with high‐status partners, limiting their ability to improve their status position. In contrast, VCs that expand across industries in a more consistent way, where moves build on prior experience and reflect a clear investment thesis, are more likely to be viewed as committed and capable, which facilitates upward status mobility. papers.title: Accommodation in the vertical supply chain: Implications of manufacturer dual tracking
papers.abstract: Research Summary The prevalence of dual tracking, in which upstream manufacturers simultaneously produce branded and private‐label products for downstream retailers, has increased substantially in recent years, driven by growing consumer demand for private‐label products. This paper examines the implications of manufacturer dual tracking by exploiting a setting in the ready‐to‐eat breakfast cereal industry where a leading branded manufacturer began supplying both products to retailers. We find that, because of this change in the vertical relationship, private‐label product introductions and advertising declined for products that directly imitated the dual‐tracking manufacturer's branded products. Changes in retailer behavior suggest that retailers accommodated the dual‐tracking manufacturer by selectively adjusting their private‐label portfolios. Dual tracking can therefore improve a manufacturer's bargaining position against retailers and reduce downstream imitation. Managerial Summary Manufacturers have increasingly produced not only their own branded products but also private‐label products for retailers that compete with those brands. This phenomenon, known as dual tracking, carries benefits and risks for manufacturers. While producing private‐label products can utilize excess capacity, these products directly compete with the branded counterpart. We study the implications for firms engaging in dual tracking and show that doing so gives manufacturers greater bargaining power in their relationships with retailers. Firms can leverage this change in bargaining power to reduce imitation by retailers' private‐label products, lessening competition concerns. Our results show that retailers reduced the introduction and advertising of private‐label products that directly compete with the dual‐tracking manufacturer.
papers.summary: Research Summary The prevalence of dual tracking, in which upstream manufacturers simultaneously produce branded and private‐label products for downstream retailers, has increased substantially in recent years, driven by growing consumer demand for private‐label products.

papers.title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
papers.abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. papers.title: Wrongdoers or Saviors? CEO Activism, Media Partisanship, and the Media’s Construction of CEO Infamy and Celebrity
papers.abstract: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity. Moving beyond conceptualizations of infamy as merely negative celebrity, we argue that infamy emerges through simple melodramatic narratives casting CEOs as wrongdoers, whereas celebrity involves more complex dramatized narratives portraying CEOs as saviors. Focusing on CEOs’ liberal sociopolitical activism—a visible, ideologically-charged action that departs from conventional executive roles—we theorize that this behavior generates divergent constructions in partisan media: infamy in conservative outlets and celebrity in liberal outlets. We further argue that activism more readily generates infamy than celebrity because melodramatic narratives are simpler to construct and negative deviance is more readily perceived than positive deviance. We examine two moderators of these relationships. Firm performance differentially shapes these constructions, with poorer performance intensifying conservative-media infamy and stronger performance amplifying liberal-media celebrity. CEO social media engagement, conversely, attenuates both by constraining traditional media’s narrative discretion and reducing activism’s newsworthiness. We develop an LLM-based annotation system capturing CEO-directed sentiment, role attributions, and dramaturgical narratives in media articles. Analyzing 91,608 articles covering 705 S&P 500 CEOs across 45 ideologically polarized U.S. media outlets between 2016 and 2022, we find broad support for our hypotheses across our main and extensive supplemental analyses. Our findings advance understanding of CEO infamy and social evaluations more generally by revealing how partisan media construct divergent social evaluations of the same executive behavior through distinct narrative processes.
papers.summary: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity.

papers.title: Strategic search: Adaptation of internal fit and market positioning under competition
papers.abstract: Research Summary Firms seeking competitive advantage need both internal fit and a distinctive market position, yet strategy research says little about how the search for the two is related. We develop a model of strategic search that integrates an NK landscape with differentiated Cournot competition, allowing a firm's position to shape both its internal fit and distinctiveness. We show that, under low complexity, competition constrains search, locking firms into resource configurations and creating a trade‐off between internal fit and distinctiveness. Conversely, under high‐complexity competition drives distant search, so that internal fit and distinctiveness go hand‐in‐hand. We further show that competitive lock‐in constrains search by early leaders, while distant search drives the emergence of new leaders, thus offering a search‐based theory of market disruption. Managerial Summary How does the search for operationally effective configurations of resources and capabilities affect the distinctiveness of a firm's offering, and vice versa? Our work suggests that the need for distinctiveness may constrain search close to rivals but also enable the discovery of effective configurations far away from them. In relatively simple environments, where firms tend to converge on the same relatively obvious configurations, the search for distinctiveness is constraining, but in more complex environments it may enable the discovery of superior configurations. Further, early leaders may be constrained in their search as rivals cluster around them, while early followers may benefit more from distant search, potentially leading to a disruption of the market as early success proves constraining.
papers.summary: Research Summary Firms seeking competitive advantage need both internal fit and a distinctive market position, yet strategy research says little about how the search for the two is related.

papers.title: Investors' ideology and corporate symbolic and substantive climate actions
papers.abstract: Research Summary Prior research suggests that institutional investors' liberalism is associated with firms' engagement in environmental sustainability, yet whether this association manifests in symbolic or substantive actions remains unclear. Taking a question‐driven approach, our analyses of Russell 3000 firms (2010–2020) reveal that investor liberalism, measured as the proportion of donations made to the Democratic Party, is positively associated with symbolic climate actions only from 2016 onward (a period when political polarization intensified), reversing a negative association during 2010–2015. Its positive association with substantive actions from 2016 onward, however, appears only among consistent Democratic donors (stronger liberal values), among dedicated investors, or in firms without CEO duality (greater investor influence). These findings indicate that liberal investor ownership may encourage, rather than deter, firms' environmental decoupling. Managerial Summary Liberal institutional investors tend to favor greater corporate environmental sustainability efforts, but are they associated with firms' symbolic or substantive climate actions? Our findings based on U.S. firms reveal that across the full 2010–2020 period, firms with more liberal investors, as indicated by their Democratic‐leaning political donations, do not exhibit more symbolic or substantive climate actions. From 2016 onward, as political polarization intensified, firms with more liberal investors exhibited more symbolic climate actions but not substantive ones. During this period, only investors with stronger liberal commitment (i.e., consistent Democratic donors) are associated with more substantive actions. Democratic‐donating investors are also associated with more substantive actions when they are dedicated investors or when firm CEOs do not chair their boards.
papers.summary: Research Summary Prior research suggests that institutional investors' liberalism is associated with firms' engagement in environmental sustainability, yet whether this association manifests in symbolic or substantive actions remains unclear.

papers.title: Two-Sided Search in International Markets
Connectors and Influencers
papers.abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. papers.title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
papers.abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06826 .
papers.summary: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior.

papers.title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
papers.abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. We also find that unconditional model rankings closely mirror those in bull markets, overstating the superiority of the models identified as best performing in expansions by ignoring the performance convergence across models that emerges in downturns. This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04942 .
papers.summary: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts.

papers.title: Effortful vs. Opportunistic Consumption of Discretionary Time: How Time-Reporting Decisions Influence Extra-Role Effort
papers.abstract: Employees often work under incomplete contracts, performing both contracted in-role tasks and valuable but noncontracted extra-role activities. Once employees have completed in-role tasks, discretionary time remains, which they may allocate to extra-role activities or consume opportunistically. This study examines how managers’ time-reporting decisions, as a less intrusive form of control, affect subordinates’ effort-allocation decisions. I propose two opposing predictions. First, managers’ control implementations may signal distrust, resulting in more opportunism and thus less extra-role effort. Second, I identify value signaling as a novel theoretical mechanism through which time-reporting decisions may increase extra-role effort. The main experiment manipulated two factors: the type of time report (aggregated versus disaggregated) and its implementation source (managerial choice versus random assignment) to isolate signaling effects from monitoring effects. Results reveal that when managers choose not to implement disaggregated time reporting—that is, reports that make discretionary time salient—subordinates significantly reduce their extra-role effort. Structural equation modeling shows that value signaling outweighs distrust signaling in driving employees’ effort-allocation decisions. In contrast, when the time-reporting format is randomly assigned, effort remains unchanged, underscoring the signaling role of managerial choice. An additional online experiment shows directionally consistent results with the main experiment. These findings reveal a hidden cost of not controlling and contribute to the literature on incomplete contracts, slack resources, and input-based controls in modern work contexts. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: This work was supported by the Bijzonder Onderzoeksfonds UGent [Grant BOF/STA/202009/047]. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00955 .
papers.summary: Employees often work under incomplete contracts, performing both contracted in-role tasks and valuable but noncontracted extra-role activities.

papers.title: Can Voluntary Corporate Transparency Curb Corruption? Community-Level Evidence from Oil and Gas Fields in Africa
papers.abstract: Voluntary corporate transparency seeks to promote accountability through disclosure, but substantive reporting does not by itself guarantee societal benefits. We examine whether this form of self-regulation can help curb corruption where formal oversight is weak, focusing on corporate support for the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI), a multistakeholder initiative that promotes disclosure of company payments to host governments. We link geolocated data on African oil and gas fields and their operators to Afrobarometer surveys and satellite nighttime-light measures and estimate difference-in-differences models that track changes in outcomes around the same fields before and after operators endorse the EITI. We find that corporate EITI support is associated with lower perceived corruption and less reported bribery, greater civic engagement, greater perceived freedom to speak, and higher nighttime-light intensity, a proxy for local economic activity. The association with lower perceived corruption is stronger around fields with nearby NGO or aid-project activity, among residents living closer to fields, and among frequent users of traditional news media. Supplementary analyses provide indirect evidence that supporting firms were more transparent before mandatory disclosure laws took effect, and show that they had fewer joint-venture partners and larger ownership stakes after endorsement. Archival cases from Nigeria and Ghana illustrate how civil-society organizations and journalists use extractive-industry information to question firms and public authorities. The findings point to local governance benefits of voluntary transparency commitments and are consistent with an information-to-accountability account in which these benefits depend on both substantive reporting and local opportunities to scrutinize and use the information.
papers.summary: Voluntary corporate transparency seeks to promote accountability through disclosure, but substantive reporting does not by itself guarantee societal benefits.

papers.title: Does innovation success need advocacy? Stakeholder involvement in firm innovation
papers.abstract: Research Summary Prior research documents that firms often collaborate with advocacy groups to mitigate stakeholder contention. Integrating stakeholder theory into a performance model of collaborative innovation, we propose an overlooked explanation for such collaborations: to enhance the adoption of firms' innovations. We argue that advocacy groups influence the adoption of innovations through a distinct, role‐based legitimacy mechanism. Because advocacy groups are expected to scrutinize firms' conduct, their willingness to collaborate provides a credible signal that a firm's innovation is socially appropriate. These signals become particularly valuable when firms have previously faced media criticism for socially irresponsible products or services and in industries characterized by high variation in corporate social performance. Using a unique dataset on firms' innovation collaborations in Germany, we find support for our conjectures. Managerial Summary Research indicates that firms collaborate with advocacy groups to avoid boycotts or protests. We introduce a largely overlooked additional rationale for such collaborations: to enhance the adoption of a firm's innovations. We suggest that advocacy groups can lend legitimacy to innovations and argue that firms benefit most from such collaborations when their products and services received bad press in the past and when there is considerable variation in corporate social performance across firms in the industry. Based on unique data on innovation collaborations between firms and advocacy groups, we find that these conditions matter in determining when firms can significantly benefit from involving advocacy groups in their innovation projects.
papers.summary: Research Summary Prior research documents that firms often collaborate with advocacy groups to mitigate stakeholder contention.

papers.title: Platform development in incumbent firms: The interplay of data and actor interests in adding platforms to existing businesses
papers.abstract: Research Summary Despite growing interest in platform transitions, limited research examines how firms navigate challenges of building platform businesses alongside existing products. Through a longitudinal case study of a financial services firm launching a platform, we develop a process model revealing how data bottlenecks shape platform development. These bottlenecks arise from the interplay of technological limitations and control tensions over data aggregation, sharing, and usage. We identify five sequential bottlenecks, where resolving one reconfigures constraints, giving rise to the next. We theorize how data heterogeneity, variation in strategic sensitivity, and actors' absorptive capacity create opportunities for platform sponsors to capture value without competing with complementors. We extend resource dependency theory by showing how peripheral units overcome power imbalances by demonstrating value creation potential with limited data. Managerial Summary When established firms launch platforms alongside existing product businesses, they face significant data‐related obstacles. Drawing on a four‐year study of a financial services firm building a platform connecting SMEs with lenders, we show how firms must navigate challenges in collecting data from internal units and customers, making incompatible data sources work together, and persuading partners to share and use data in new ways. We find that these obstacles emerge in sequence, where resolving one creates the conditions for the next. We also find that not all data is equally useful to all partners, and that these differences can open market segments the platform sponsor can serve without competing with its own partners. Managers can maintain momentum by combining short‐term data workarounds with longer‐term structural solutions.
papers.summary: Research Summary Despite growing interest in platform transitions, limited research examines how firms navigate challenges of building platform businesses alongside existing products.

papers.title: Designing for unanticipated uses: How product attributes shape community‐led exaptation
papers.abstract: Research Summary Users often discover new uses for products that firms may later commercialize, which we call community‐led exaptation. We examine how product attributes shape users' discovery of new functions versus new functionalities. Using 1925 IKEA product hacks, we find that modularity increases the likelihood of new functions. This effect strengthens when product components are compatible across product lines but weakens when esthetic product variants exist. Visual simplicity, conversely, increases the likelihood of new functionalities. These findings suggest that firms can structure the opportunity space for discovery through product design. Exploratory analysis of archival data and interviews further illustrates how IKEA responds to these discoveries. We contribute to exaptation, user innovation, and design research by showing how product attributes shape the types of new uses communities discover. Managerial Summary How can firms design products to facilitate community‐led exaptation? We find that product attributes can shape what users discover. Modular products enable users to find new functions (i.e., applications), while visually simple products enable users to find new functionalities (i.e., new product capabilities). Firms' decisions to offer components that are compatible across product lines and esthetic product variants can influence the likelihood of new functions. Additionally, firms can capitalize on these new uses by showcasing promising community‐discovered functions on official channels or incorporate them as complements to existing product lines. However, functional modifications can raise safety concerns and may require additional development. Firms should therefore design for intended use, and for the kinds of new uses they are willing to seed and commercialize.
papers.summary: Research Summary Users often discover new uses for products that firms may later commercialize, which we call community‐led exaptation. We examine how product attributes shape users' discovery of new functions versus new functionalities.

papers.title: Are client ties pre‐entry resources? Performance implications of client tie diversification
papers.abstract: Research Summary This study investigates client tie diversification, where firms enter markets with existing clients. Recognizing the theoretical basis for both positive and negative performance implications, the paper adopts a question‐driven approach and discovers a strong negative correlation between client tie diversification and firm performance. Using data from the US federal lobbying industry during the creation of the Homeland Security issue market post‐9/11, I find that lobbying firms entering the new market with existing clients underperform compared to other firms. This underperformance is associated with over‐embeddedness with clients and agency costs from dispersed client tie ownership among lobbyists. These findings challenge the notion that client ties are readily fungible and highlight relational and agency‐related complexities that can lead firms to pursue value‐destroying diversification. Managerial Summary Do firms perform better when they diversify into new markets with their existing clients, or by pursuing new opportunities independently? This study found that firms that enter new markets alongside their current clients often underperform compared to those that do not. While it might seem beneficial to leverage existing client relationships, this approach can push firms into areas where they lack capabilities, create inefficiencies, and complicate relationships with other clients, leading to weaker performance. Managers should be cautious about letting client needs drive diversification decisions. Prioritizing current clients may offer short‐term gains but can limit the firm's ability to explore new markets and achieve long‐term growth. Strategic choices should balance client requests with the firm's own strengths and future prospects.
papers.summary: Research Summary This study investigates client tie diversification, where firms enter markets with existing clients.

papers.title: The Welfare Effects of Price Shocks and Household Relief Packages: Evidence from an Energy Crisis
papers.abstract: Aggregate price shocks generate unequal welfare losses both across and within income groups.Policymakers face a trade-off: price subsidies direct more support to households facing larger losses, but create inefficiencies, while transfers are less distortionary but harder to target.We develop and implement a framework to quantify this trade-off using rich panel data on households' energy spending and incomes, alongside price and policy variation from the 2022-23 European Energy Crisis.Absent policy intervention, average household welfare losses would have equalled 6% of income, with some households facing much larger losses.The combination of an energy-price subsidy and universal transfers reduced both the mean and dispersion of losses, but incurred efficiency costs equal to 12% of total relief-package revenue costs.Optimal policy entails a strictly positive price subsidy, though its level is lower when transfers can be targeted using income and prior energy usage.

papers.title: Geographic Integration and Firm Exports: Evidence from China,
papers.abstract: Domestic connectivity via passenger transport infrastructure can affect a country’s exports by easing information frictions. We study this mechanism using China’s high-speed rail network, which connects cities to same-sector exporters in other cities without directly affecting freight costs. Stronger connections increase firms’ export sales and expand both destination and product scope, with no change in domestic sales, total employment, or shipping costs. The effects are largest for firms facing greater information barriers. Connected firms upgrade product quality and their export destinations converge toward those of newly connected peers, with initially weaker firms converging toward stronger connected peers while stronger firms show little adjustment. A within-firm cross-destination specification confirms that improved connectivity generates destination-specific benefits. The results point to an information-based channel through which passenger connectivity affects trade, including knowledge about export markets and inputs.
papers.journal: Journal of the European Economic Association
papers.summary: Domestic connectivity via passenger transport infrastructure can affect a country’s exports by easing information frictions.

papers.title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
papers.abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01302 .
papers.summary: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics.

papers.title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
papers.abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Evidence from firms’ biodiversity dependencies suggests that physical biodiversity risks are also priced in the bond market. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07660 .
papers.summary: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021.

papers.title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
papers.abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we caution that a more efficient waste valorization process may lead to negative outcomes for both the manufacturer and the environment. This analysis not only sheds light on how waste valorization contributes to waste reduction and economic value, but also provides insights for production decision making. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Financial support from the National Science Foundation of China [Grants 72301055, 72322017, 72471244, and 72101102] is gratefully
papers.summary: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention.

papers.title: Firm divisionalization and the gender gap in CEO promotion
papers.abstract: Research Summary This study examines how divisionalized firm structures shape the gender gap in internal chief executive officer (CEO) promotion. We argue that divisionalized firms may narrow the gender gap in CEO succession by generating more individually attributable performance information about senior managers. In contrast to firms in which candidates' contributions are difficult to isolate, divisionalized firms create profit‐and‐loss (P&L) accountability that makes managerial performance more visible and comparable. Using longitudinal data on over 616,000 managers in 49,135 US firms, we find that women are more likely to be promoted to CEO in divisionalized firms. We also find that the gender gap is smaller among managers with prior P&L‐accountable experience. Among managers in divisionalized firms, stronger unit performance relative to within‐firm peers is more positively associated with promotion to CEO for women than for men. The results highlight organizational structure as a potential source of variation in gender inequality in executive advancement. Managerial Summary Why do so few women become CEOs? Part of the answer lies in how firms are organized. When a company is structured into divisions with their own profit‐and‐loss responsibility, the results of the managers who lead those units are easier to observe, compare, and credit to the individual. This leaves less room for subjective judgments through which gender bias often enters promotion decisions. In data on more than 600,000 managers at roughly 49,000 US firms, we find that women are more likely to be promoted to CEO in divisionalized firms. The pattern is strongest for women who have led a business unit, and strong unit results count for more in women's promotion prospects. For boards seeking greater gender equity in CEO succession, structures and evaluation systems that give senior leaders clear, comparable performance records may matter as much as diversity initiatives.
papers.summary: Research Summary This study examines how divisionalized firm structures shape the gender gap in internal chief executive officer (CEO) promotion.

papers.title: Strategy as a theory of change
papers.abstract: Research Summary The theory‐based view argues that a strategist's task is to develop a theory to move the organization to an improved future state. Focusing on theorizing as a thought process of model creation, we propose a framework to specify hypothetical causal links and analyze their structure as a directed graph connecting inputs, activities, and indicators of problem resolution. We then propose a set of metrics operationalizing key theory attributes: complexity, equifinality, interdependence, and circularity. We discuss the strategic relevance of these attributes in terms of a theory's ability to promote comprehensive problem resolution as well as implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed solution. Our work represents a step toward operationalizing model creation in the theory‐based view and informs the design of strategic theories of change. Managerial Summary Strategists often theorize how to move their organizations toward an improved performance state. Yet most strategic analysis tools describe the organization's external environment or the internal components of its business model, without precisely specifying forward‐looking interventions that might cause the desired changes. In this paper, we represent strategic theories as a chain of causal interventions—inputs and activities that address relevant problems and lead to desirable outcomes. We propose a structured framework that helps managers develop theories and measure key attributes that influence comprehensive problem resolution and the ability to implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed interventions. In this sense, our work helps managers mentally create their strategic theories and assess their usefulness as a roadmap to superior performance.
papers.summary: Research Summary The theory‐based view argues that a strategist's task is to develop a theory to move the organization to an improved future state.

papers.title: Beliefs and the Incentive Effects of Preferential College Admissions: Evidence from an Experiment and a Structural Model
Noisy Global Value Chains
Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany
papers.abstract: Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced assortative matching between workers and firms, lowered the skill premium, and weakened firms’ monopsony power.
papers.summary: Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession.

papers.title: Aspiring to a Better Future: Can a Simple Psychological Intervention Reduce Poverty?
papers.abstract: Do higher aspirations for the future motivate people living in poverty to make long-term investments? Do their aspirations increase when economic conditions improve? To answer these questions, we run a 415-village field experiment with 8,300 women living in poverty in rural Kenya. We design an 80-minute workshop to help people set higher aspirations and plan to achieve them. We cross-randomise this with large unconditional cash transfers. The workshop substantially raises aspirations, labour supply, investment, revenue, and living standards 17 months later, relative to a placebo workshop. Increases in aspirations are the most likely mechanism to explain the economic effects. Cash transfers also raise aspirations, which might help to explain why transfers increase labour supply and investment. We conclude that aspirations respond to both economic and psychological interventions, contribute to investment decisions and living standards, and are important considerations for development policy.
papers.summary: Do higher aspirations for the future motivate people living in poverty to make long-term investments? Do their aspirations increase when economic conditions improve?

papers.title: Daddy’s Girl: Daughters, Managerial Decisions, and Gender Inequality
papers.abstract: Using Danish registry data, we study how managers’ gender attitudes shape gender inequality in the workplace by exploiting the birth of a daughter—as opposed to a son—as a plausibly exogenous shock to male managers’ gender attitudes. Comparing within-firm changes in women’s labour outcomes depending on the gender of the manager’s newborn child, we find that women’s relative earnings and employment increase by 4.4% and 2.9%, respectively, following the birth of the manager’s first daughter. These effects are driven by an increase in managers’ propensity to substitute male hires with female hires that have comparable education, hours worked, and earnings. Consistent with this substitution channel, we do not detect any significant effect on firm performance. Because these effects emerge rapidly and persist over time, we can rule out the need for prolonged exposure to gender issues or for personal incentives tied to improving conditions for their own daughters as prerequisites for managers to promote gender equality within their firms.
papers.summary: Using Danish registry data, we study how managers’ gender attitudes shape gender inequality in the workplace by exploiting the birth of a daughter—as opposed to a son—as a plausibly exogenous shock to male managers’ gender attitudes.

papers.title: Learning‐by‐twinning: Organizational digital twins and the future of search
papers.abstract: Research Summary Entrepreneurs and managers often need to evaluate strategic choices, such as redesigning an incentive plan or entering an unfamiliar market, before committing scarce resources. Existing offline search tools, including mental models, analogical reasoning, model building, and simulation, allow managers to weigh alternatives without acting, but each is limited by what a single decision maker can specify, recall, or imagine. We argue that advances in generative AI, combined with the growing availability of firm‐specific digital trace data, are transforming this tradeoff. We introduce the organizational digital twin (ODT), an infrastructure combining firm‐specific data, AI‐based behavioral simulation models, and governance rules which facilitates a new form of offline search that we call learning‐by‐twinning: search conducted by observing how a strategic choice unfolds within a digital replica of the firm. We identify three mechanisms through which learning‐by‐twinning creates value, namely expanded search, safer experimentation, and richer system‐level feedback as well as specify certain conditions under which these benefits may attenuate.
