Enabled by advances in generative artificial intelligence and organizational data infrastructures, we theorize that a new form of entrepreneurial search—learning‐by‐twinning—allows managers to conduct systematic virtual experimentation prior to real‐world implementation. We introduce the concept of the organizational digital twin (ODT) as the technological infrastructure that makes this search and experimentation possible: an evolving simulation environment built from firm‐specific digital trace data and multi‐agent AI models capable of reproducing organizational routines, interactions, and decision processes. papers.title: Generative AI use in entrepreneurship: An integrative review and the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework
papers.abstract: Research Summary Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative, entrepreneur‐centered review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework, which not only catalogs GenAI's benefits and costs throughout the entrepreneurial process but also identifies potential trade‐offs underlying GenAI's double‐edged role. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality yet produce hallucinations and biases; boost entrepreneurial self‐efficacy yet heighten overconfidence; increase functional breadth and self‐sufficiency yet reduce prosociality; and enhance productivity yet diminish cognitive engagement, learning, and memory. We also identify features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. Moreover, we explore boundary conditions that moderate GenAI's effects, including entrepreneurs' expertise, approaches to GenAI use, and personal traits and values. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and framework offer practical guidance for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically while managing its risks. Managerial Summary We review how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: opportunity recognition and ideation, opportunity evaluation and commitment, resource assembly and mobilization, and venture launch and growth. Based on this review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework to help entrepreneurs understand GenAI's trade‐offs at each stage. papers.title: Generative AI and the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantages
papers.abstract: Research Summary This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantage. We argue that GenAI's impact is conditional on how those opportunities are formed. Discovery opportunities originate from exogenous industry shocks. However, widely available GenAI tools are likely to commoditize opportunity recognition in these settings and thus reduce advantages that might have been generated by exploiting these opportunities. Creation opportunities emerge endogenously, under conditions of Knightian uncertainty, through entrepreneurial action and interaction with the environment. However, GenAI cannot fully resolve the Knightian uncertainty inherent in creation settings, so sustained advantage here depends on whether resources and capabilities developed through creating an opportunity are inimitable. Unawareness opportunities rely on competitive neglect. GenAI may reduce the advantages of firms in these settings when it makes rents legible to potential competitors and when search is directed toward these invisible markets. Whether GenAI can create sustained competitive advantages, this paper argues, depends on how an opportunity is formed. When opportunities arise from entrepreneurs noticing an external market shift, GenAI levels the playing field by commoditizing recognition and pushes entrepreneurs to win through execution and hard‐to‐copy complements. papers.title: When machines learn with organizations: AI‐enabled knowledge creation and entrepreneurship
papers.abstract: Research Summary To promote entrepreneurship and new business development, firms will increasingly rely on new forms of knowledge creation to manage environments marked by technological change and radical uncertainty. We argue that as generative artificial intelligence (Gen‐AI) becomes embedded in organizational processes, knowledge creation will no longer remain solely a human activity. Instead, it will increasingly emerge from hybrid interactions between human actors and firm‐specific, closed Gen‐AI systems. These systems begin to participate directly in how knowledge is generated, recombined, internalized, shared, and converted into entrepreneurial initiatives such as corporate entrepreneurship, spin‐offs, and new business models. We also reconceptualize organizational knowledge creation as a hybrid human–AI process and propose a reordered knowledge creation cycle that induces multiple knowledge spirals, captures the emergence of new agents, and the generation of diverse types of knowledge, with faster temporal dynamics. Building on this perspective, we offer a research agenda for future scholarship. Managerial Summary We discuss how firm‐specific generative AI systems are likely to fundamentally alter the ways firms generate knowledge, respond to change, and sustain long‐term renewal. We propose that rather than replacing human judgment, closed Gen‐AI changes where knowledge originates as well as how quickly it evolves, and how broadly it circulates across organizational boundaries. This means that the managerial challenge is less about adopting AI and more about designing knowledge systems and structuring knowledge flows. Executives and entrepreneurs alike need to decide how to structure human–AI collaborations, how much autonomy to grant closed Gen‐AI systems, and how to prevent speed from overwhelming sensemaking. papers.title: Artificial intelligence and venture capital: Revisiting sourcing, selection, and nurturing activities
papers.abstract: Research Summary Venture capital (VC) is an information‐intensive form of entrepreneurial finance conducted under extreme uncertainty. Investors must originate promising opportunities, select ventures with sparse and strategically disclosed information, and monitor and support firms after investment. Prior research documents both formal mechanisms (e.g., staged financing, syndication) and informal mechanisms built on referrals, reputation, and constant interaction. Geographic and social proximity enable these mechanisms by lowering the cost of obtaining contextual information and coordinating action. We develop a mechanism‐based account of how data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) reconfigure this established model. Our framework yields propositions on geographic dispersion in sourcing, portfolio selection, and the distinct effects of AI on monitoring versus value‐added support. It also identifies boundary conditions associated with institutional setting and heterogeneous AI adoption. Managerial Summary For venture capital firms, AI is not a single tool and adoption is not a binary choice. A fund may use data systems to identify founders, machine‐learning models to organize deal flow, generative AI to summarize diligence materials, or analytics to monitor portfolio companies. Each application changes a different part of the VC process. In sourcing, AI can widen the funnel beyond warm introductions and local ecosystems, especially in sectors such as software and e‐commerce where hiring, product, and customer signals are visible. In selection, AI can make diligence faster and more consistent, but models trained on past investments may favor ventures that resemble previously funded companies and may miss novel opportunities for which historical analogues are weak. papers.title: Entrepreneurship and Financial Deregulation
papers.abstract: We quantitatively analyze the impact of US banking deregulation in the 1980s on the aggregate economy. Using recent econometric techniques, we first reexamine existing empirical evidence on the real effects of banking deregulation. We then construct a quantitative model that integrates imperfectly competitive banks into a general equilibrium framework of firm dynamics and occupational choice. Consistent with the empirical evidence, deregulation significantly increases output growth and firm entry. Increased competition among banks and the entrepreneurs' occupational choices play an important role in shaping the economy's response to deregulation.
papers.summary: We quantitatively analyze the impact of US banking deregulation in the 1980s on the aggregate economy. Using recent econometric techniques, we first reexamine existing empirical evidence on the real effects of banking deregulation.

papers.title: Entrepreneurial theorizing with generative artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear. On the one hand, LLMs may help entrepreneurs build more developed causal structures and surface diverse information that supports the formulation of distinctive theories. On the other hand, LLMs may steer causal structures toward conventional forms and discourage the counterintuitive reasoning needed to develop distinctive theories. In a within‐subject experiment with 199 participants theorizing both with and without LLM assistance, we find no significant average treatment effect on either structural or content properties. However, this null average effect masks a redistribution effect, where LLM assistance supplemented theorizing when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive but displaced participants' own theorizing when their theories were already more developed or distinctive. Managerial Summary Large language models (LLMs) can help entrepreneurs develop business ideas by surfacing knowledge across domains and sharpening causal logic. At the same time, LLMs may also push reasoning toward conventional patterns and away from the counterintuitive ideas that are a source of breakthrough opportunities. In a study of 199 participants theorizing with and without LLM assistance, we find that LLMs supported the development of causal structure and content distinctiveness when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive, whereas they had the opposite effect when those theories were already more developed or distinctive. This suggests that while LLMs can scaffold entrepreneurs still developing their theories, greater caution is warranted for those whose theories are already more developed or distinctive, as assistance may diminish those properties.
papers.summary: Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear.

papers.title: The intelligence loop and value creation in the age of AI agents
papers.abstract: Research Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from generating outputs to executing work. An agent that executes work autonomously produces something generative AI does not: operational experience that can raise its future intelligence. Prior research on AI emphasizes value creation through demand‐side feedback, notably data network effects, in which user data improve prediction and reinforce adoption. We develop the supply‐side counterpart, the intelligence loop: delegated usage generates operational experience, agentic capability converts it into future intelligence, and the resulting value maintains or expands usage. The loop cannot operate until autonomous execution is viable, a threshold we call minimum viable intelligence (MVI). Crossing MVI does not guarantee rising intelligence. Comparable deployments of AI agents can diverge as their loops decay, sustain, or accelerate. Three implications follow. Competitive advantage may depend more on the loop than on installed base. An above‐MVI agent supplies scarce expert skill as a non‐rival, replicable resource, so productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount, with the one‐person company as a limiting case. And a venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can still fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. An agent crosses a workflow's minimum viable intelligence (MVI) when it executes reliably without step‐by‐step direction, autonomous execution creates at least as much net value as the best alternative after oversight and correction costs, and governance arrangements keep residual risk acceptable and accountability clear. papers.title: “Borrowing intelligence to build a business”: The promise of open‐source AI for entrepreneurship
papers.abstract: Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.
papers.summary: Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity.

papers.title: New wine, old bottles? Effective strategies of new GenAI firms
papers.abstract: Research Summary Blending insights from GenAI, strategic reasoning, and empirical grounding in five illustrative ventures, we contribute a theoretical framework for effective strategies of new GenAI firms. They face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory) such that two complementary strategic logics—Process Perspective (PP) and Resource‐based View (RBV)—are relevant. Second, we identify process‐based (i.e., well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. Some relate to GenAI, some generalize. Third, we address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI, technology strategy when there is upstream technical dominance and many downstream firms, and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software and predictive AI. Managerial Summary The rapid trajectory of GenAI is stunning. Yet many new GenAI firms are simply thin wrappers around well‐known LLMs. Drawing on five illustrative ventures, we contribute a framework for effective strategies for new GenAI firms. These firms face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory). This calls for creating advantage by navigating high uncertainty markets to accomplish key strategic tasks and relying on foresight to build strategically valuable resources. Specifically, we identify process‐based (well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. We also address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software, predictive AI, and quantum.
papers.summary: Research Summary Blending insights from GenAI, strategic reasoning, and empirical grounding in five illustrative ventures, we contribute a theoretical framework for effective strategies of new GenAI firms.

papers.title: Generative AI and the architecture of knowledge work: Expertise bypass, exchange governability, and shifting bottlenecks
papers.abstract: Research Summary Research on GenAI and work has largely focused on tasks. We ask when task‐level effects alter knowledge‐work industry architecture: the allocation of activities across firm boundaries. Using a three‐stage abductive design—an executive roundtable, a panel of 626 firm websites (2017–2025), and 33 interviews plus two further roundtables with C‐level executives and corporate directors—we document divergent repositioning: professional services firms foreground relational value, while interface‐oriented technology firms emphasize scalable interfaces. We find that activity reallocation is shaped by two independently varying dimensions: expertise bypass and exchange governability. Their intersection yields four configurations: contestable reallocation, persistent bundles with selective insourcing, federated expert provision, and integrated expert provision. We extend industry architecture theory by explaining change when production and exchange conditions shift separately. Managerial Summary GenAI is not simply making knowledge work more efficient—it may be changing which organizations perform which work. We document that professional services firms are emphasizing relationship‐driven, judgment‐intensive work, while interface‐oriented technology firms are extending scalable delivery. Our framework explains why task exposure alone does not determine where work moves. We distinguish between expertise bypass—whether GenAI can produce an output without the expertise previously required—and exchange governability—whether that activity can be specified, verified, priced, and warranted across firm boundaries. Where both are present, work becomes contestable and may be reallocated. Where they diverge, highly exposed activities may remain bundled, while less exposed, human‐intensive work may move through federated specialist models. These conditions shape which organizational forms become viable.
papers.summary: Research Summary Research on GenAI and work has largely focused on tasks. We ask when task‐level effects alter knowledge‐work industry architecture: the allocation of activities across firm boundaries.

papers.title: Conceptual search: A generative view of entrepreneurial imagination
papers.abstract: Research Summary Entrepreneurs cannot pursue ventures they never imagine. This article develops a generative view of entrepreneurial imagination as the construction of an evolving candidate set through generation, provisional evaluation, and revision. Conceptual search represents venture concepts as text, transforms them through interpretable operations, and compares their promise. A large language model prototype demonstrates complementary modes: local refinement lifts a concept from sixteenth to third among 30 ventures under a validated evaluator, while global recombination reaches distant possibilities that refinement makes competitive. The framework shows how search architecture determines what enters, survives, and develops, and how AI may broaden imagination within firms while producing correlated imagination across firms. By making imagination programmable, auditable, and experimentally tractable, conceptual search opens a research program on how entrepreneurial possibilities are constructed. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs can pursue only the ventures they imagine, and valuable ideas routinely go unbuilt because nobody thinks of them. AI makes imagining cheap: it can draft, critique, and rewrite venture concepts in seconds, so developing ideas becomes a process that can be designed, run, and audited. I demonstrate a system that evolves real venture concepts: step‐by‐step refinement lifted a middling concept to third place among 30 real ventures, as ranked by an AI judge shown to predict fundraising, while recombining distant ideas created novel concepts that refinement made competitive. The entrepreneur's job shifts from generating a few ideas to governing many: choosing what to search, keep, and test in the market. One caution: rivals using the same AI will imagine similar ventures; advantage comes from proprietary problems, data, and evidence.
papers.summary: Research Summary Entrepreneurs cannot pursue ventures they never imagine. This article develops a generative view of entrepreneurial imagination as the construction of an evolving candidate set through generation, provisional evaluation, and revision.

papers.title: Value creation and capture in artificial intelligence‐enabled ecosystems
papers.abstract: Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.
papers.summary: Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology.

papers.title: Labor Market Monopsony Power and the Dynamic Gains to Openness Reforms
papers.abstract: We embed labor market monopsony into a dynamic heterogeneous‐firm general equilibrium model with exporting, horizontal FDI, and rich firm lifecycle dynamics. Rising marginal costs with monopsony slow and limit incumbent firm growth in response to liberalization, shifting adjustment to the extensive margin. Calibrated to US micro data, welfare gains from tariff reduction are over four times larger under monopsony than with perfect labor markets. The difference is mostly driven by new exporter creation and firm entry along the transition path. By contrast, lowering outward FDI taxes gives powerful quantitative welfare losses under monopsony, as firms undertake FDI to escape domestic wage pressure.
papers.summary: We embed labor market monopsony into a dynamic heterogeneous‐firm general equilibrium model with exporting, horizontal FDI, and rich firm lifecycle dynamics.

papers.title: Entry and Welfare in General Equilibrium With Heterogeneous Firms and Endogenous Markups
papers.abstract: We analyze market entry efficiency in single‐ and two‐sector closed‐economy Melitz–Ottaviano (MO) models without an outside good. Comparing market and second‐best outcomes, we find that market entry is efficient in the single‐sector model. This efficiency also holds in a symmetric two‐sector setting. When sectors have asymmetric demand and the level of asymmetry is sufficiently small, the market yields excessive entry into the “high‐demand” sector. This inefficiency arises from the presence of an additional aggregator in MO preferences.
papers.summary: We analyze market entry efficiency in single‐ and two‐sector closed‐economy Melitz–Ottaviano (MO) models without an outside good. Comparing market and second‐best outcomes, we find that market entry is efficient in the single‐sector model.

papers.title: Everything everywhere all‐at‐once? AI, expertise–output decoupling, and new entrepreneurial strategy trade‐offs in the age of abundance
papers.abstract: Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.
papers.summary: Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality.

papers.title: Public support and VC financing in academic startups
papers.abstract: Research Summary We investigate public support and venture capital (VC) investment in academic startups. Government support may enable follow‐on investment by providing a quality signal to investors. This signal is especially important for academic startups, which face large funding gaps due to their complexity, cutting‐edge nature, and uncertainty regarding the founders' management capabilities and commitment. Using a panel of startups in Germany, our analyses confirm that academic startups are more likely to obtain follow‐on VC investment after receiving public support than non‐academic startups. Further, this effect is limited in time, lasts longer for academic startups, is concentrated in high‐tech manufacturing firms, and is stronger for investments from business angels. Our findings have implications for policymakers seeking to foster academic entrepreneurship through policy programs and VC investment. Managerial Summary Obtaining seed and growth capital is essential for potentially highly innovative startups. We show that startups that obtain public support are more likely to receive VC funding and that this effect is stronger for startups with academic founders, approximately twice as large. We further show that this benefit is limited in time, concentrated in the high‐tech manufacturing industry, and more salient for business angel financing than for investment by independent VC funds or corporate VCs. For founders of academic startups, our results imply that acquiring public support might enhance the chances of attracting follow‐on financing.
papers.summary: Research Summary We investigate public support and venture capital (VC) investment in academic startups. Government support may enable follow‐on investment by providing a quality signal to investors.

papers.title: Startup multihoming in enterprise software ecosystems: The role of skill breadth and organizational learning
papers.abstract: Research Summary We investigate startup decisions to multihome to another platform. We develop a theory that shows startup engagement with the initial platform leads first to exploratory learning and later a shift toward exploitation, leading to an inverted U‐shape relationship between duration of platform partnership and the likelihood of multihoming. This tradeoff is shaped by the breadth of the startup's skill base. Startups with a broader set of skills initially face slower learning, but over time skill breadth provides greater adaptability that better positions them for multihoming. We test our theory using a novel dataset on SAP partners' multihoming decisions, examining the implications of Oracle acquisitions that increased the expected benefits of multihoming. Our empirical findings are consistent with our hypotheses. Managerial Summary The growth phase forms an important part of any startup's evolution, particularly when engaging with digital platform ecosystems, where expansion often depends on the ability to multihome. Startups' accumulated experience with a platform shapes how they respond when opportunities to expand to another platform arise. Startups with moderate levels of prior platform experience are most likely to expand, while longer relationships can create dependencies that reduce flexibility. Importantly, the breadth of a startup's skill base changes this trajectory. Startups with diverse skills are better able to avoid lock‐in and remain flexible, even after long partnerships. Evidence from the enterprise software ecosystem shows managers should see platform partnerships as both opportunity and risk, investing in broad skill sets to balance deep collaboration with the ability to grow across platforms.
papers.summary: Research Summary We investigate startup decisions to multihome to another platform.

papers.title: The cost of the buzz? A sufficiency threshold perspective on digital transformation disclosure and cost of equity capital
papers.abstract: Firms disclose information about complex internal activities to keep capital markets informed about their long-term value. We engage two rival predictions, the 'more-is-better' assumption in information risk theory and the 'more-is-noisy' assumption in technological fad perspectives, and ask what shape best characterizes the association between firms' digital transformation (DT) disclosure and the cost of equity capital. Using FTSE350 firms from 2010 to 2020 and adopting a question-driven, phenomenon-based approach, we document a non-linear association in which both traditions describe the same relationship over different ranges of disclosure. Where disclosure is sparse, capital markets cannot separate commitment from fashion and additional disclosure in this range is associated with a higher cost of equity capital; where disclosure becomes substantively informative, the information benefit dominates and the association reverses. The estimated sufficiency threshold, 0.0149% of annual report text, is reached by almost no firm in our sample. Prevailing disclosure practice therefore sits on the ascending portion of the association, while the descending portion is identified from a thin upper tail. The concavity of this relationship is robust to excluding the highest-disclosing firms, to winsorisation, to selection correction, and to leaving out any single firm. We discuss implications for theories of corporate disclosure of complex internal activity and for the design of DT disclosure policy.
papers.summary: Firms disclose information about complex internal activities to keep capital markets informed about their long-term value.

papers.title: Learning from success but not from failure in digital experimentation
Government‐funded experimentation: How startups use R&D contracts to resolve uncertainty
papers.abstract: Research Summary Startups use experimentation to reduce technological and market uncertainty, but experimentation is costly and unevenly funded. This paper examines how government‐funded experimentation relates to subsequent performance among high‐tech startups that receive federal awards. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups between 2001 and 2018, I distinguish between technology experimentation, measured by the value of R&D contracts, and market experimentation, measured by the number of agencies awarding the R&D contracts. Market experimentation is positively associated with subsequent employment, sales, and acquisition, while technology experimentation shows weaker associations with these outcomes. The findings are consistent with startups using information from multiple government buyers to learn about market opportunities and improve subsequent performance. Managerial Summary High‐tech startups need to test both whether their technology works and where demand exists, but venture capital often leaves this experimentation unfunded. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups from 2001 to 2018, this paper shows that startups funded by more government agencies subsequently have higher employment and sales and are more likely to be acquired. Larger R&D contract amounts have less consistent relationships with these outcomes. For managers, the findings suggest considering what different government customers can help the firm learn. For policymakers, they suggest that the diversity of a startup's public customer base is a vital margin to consider alongside the overall size of its R&D awards.
papers.summary: Research Summary Startups use experimentation to reduce technological and market uncertainty, but experimentation is costly and unevenly funded.

papers.title: It's a match! Similarity in personality traits in the business angel–founder dyad and follow‐on funding
papers.abstract: Research summary We assess how personality alignment in investor–founder dyads is associated with the likelihood of follow‐on funding, a vital outcome for early‐stage ventures. Using machine learning to infer the Big Five personality traits from Twitter data for 9497 business angel–founder dyads, we find that similarity in conscientiousness and agreeableness is associated with a higher likelihood of follow‐on funding, while similarity in neuroticism is associated with a lower likelihood. We attribute these patterns to the trait‐specific benefits of supplementary (conscientiousness and agreeableness) and complementary (neuroticism) fit. Robustness checks and additional analyses support and nuance the conclusion that personality fit matters for venture outcomes, highlighting the strategic role of personality fit in the investor–founder relationship. Managerial summary We show that personality similarity between business angels and founders is associated with whether a venture secures follow‐on funding. Similarity in conscientiousness (being organized and reliable) and agreeableness (being cooperative and trusting) is linked to a higher likelihood of securing follow‐on funding, while similarity in neuroticism (emotional instability) is linked to a lower likelihood. We interpret these patterns as collaboration dynamics: similarity can help through supplementary fit (e.g., shared work style and cooperation), but differences can help through complementary fit (e.g., one partner's emotional stability offsets the other's emotional instability). Practically, founders and business angels should develop self‐awareness and consider personality fit alongside other characteristics when forming partnerships. Policymakers and incubators can support better matches and strengthen collaboration by promoting awareness of interpersonal dynamics.
papers.summary: Research summary We assess how personality alignment in investor–founder dyads is associated with the likelihood of follow‐on funding, a vital outcome for early‐stage ventures.

papers.title: Whither business model innovation strategy in the age of AI?
papers.abstract: Research Summary We argue that business models are transformed into auto‐adaptive systems through embedded AI inference and learning activities. The competitive advantage of focal firms may increasingly depend on how effectively their activity systems learn relative to competing business models, with learning serving as a meta value driver. Such learning‐based advantages may be difficult to replicate when they are costly to create, path dependent, anchored in distinctive accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. Entrepreneurs and corporate leaders thus become architects and curators of evolving learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance. Managerial Summary The competitive advantage of focal firms increasingly depends on new AI learning and inference activities, which serve as meta‐value drivers in business models that learn faster, more broadly, and more reliably than competing business models. These dynamic learning‐based advantages are difficult to replicate because they are costly, path dependent, anchored in specific accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. In this paper we argue that entrepreneurs and corporate leaders need to become architects and curators of evolving, auto‐adaptive learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance.
papers.summary: Research Summary We argue that business models are transformed into auto‐adaptive systems through embedded AI inference and learning activities.

papers.title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
papers.abstract: Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.
papers.summary: Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past.

papers.title: Strong Nash equilibria of core-selecting double auctions
papers.abstract: We study core-selecting auctions for double auctions that incorporate package bidding. Unlike in one-sided core-selecting auctions, the core may be empty in more general double auction settings, and truncation strategies need not be amongst a bidder’s best responses. Nevertheless, we establish the existence of a core-selecting auction in which every imputation in the core with respect to true preferences corresponds to a strong Nash equilibrium. Specifically, for any core imputation, there exists a profile of truncation strategies that constitutes a strong Nash equilibrium and induces precisely that imputation.
papers.summary: We study core-selecting auctions for double auctions that incorporate package bidding.

papers.title: Framing the unknowable: The role of language and frame multiplicity in early‐stage startup pitches
papers.abstract: Research Summary Early‐stage startup pitches must make largely unknowable futures plausible. As such, they bear a rhetorical burden. This study theorizes how multiple frames jointly shape this burden and, consequently, affect investor evaluations. Specifically, it considers how future growth frames interact with concreteness and novelty frames. Evidence from 618 startup pitches and ad‐hoc investor evaluations reveals that growth frames relying more on entrepreneurs' own assertions than on established grounds tend to receive lower investor evaluations. This evaluative discount is alleviated when growth is expressed concretely but becomes more pronounced when the pitch emphasizes novelty. These findings extend framing theory by explaining the relevance and possible implications of frame multiplicity in pitches and entrepreneurial communication more broadly. Managerial Summary Mobilizing support for a new venture is difficult because founders must often describe a future that does not yet exist. This study of 618 startup pitches shows that growth‐related messages can shape investor evaluations even at the earliest stage, but only if configured well. Because growth frames must appear plausible amid the uncertainty surrounding new startups, framing early‐stage startups around growth is rhetorically burdensome. Findings show that pitches are evaluated less favorably when they rely more on founders' own projections and reasoning than on established grounds such as market analyses. Concrete language can alleviate this burden, while novelty framing intensifies it. As such, this study reveals intricate and potentially unintended interactions among multiple frames within a single pitch.
papers.summary: Research Summary Early‐stage startup pitches must make largely unknowable futures plausible. As such, they bear a rhetorical burden. This study theorizes how multiple frames jointly shape this burden and, consequently, affect investor evaluations.

papers.title: Re‐thinking academic entrepreneurship: Micro, meso, and macro perspectives
papers.abstract: Research Summary We summarize and synthesize the papers contained in the special issue and use these studies to illustrate key micro, meso, and macro dimensions of academic entrepreneurship, where micro focuses on the scientist, meso is concerned with the university ecosystem, and macro refers to the broader entrepreneurial ecosystem. A key finding from our special issue is that routines, pivots, and intellectual property, which determine venture viability, emerge from granular individual action, including identity formation and evolution. We also find that macro instruments such as public funding/grants and institutional governance appear to steer resources toward viable science‐based ventures. Our essay concludes by presenting numerous additional micro, meso, and macro research questions to motivate future research on the managerial and public policy implications of academic entrepreneurship. Managerial Summary There are several key managerial implications of our essay and this special issue. “Managers” and those who supervise academic entrepreneurs need to develop and support their scientists entrepreneurial identity formation and evolution. Managers also need to enhance incentives for academic entrepreneurship and foster a culture within their academic departments, schools, and colleges that support these activities. Policymakers need to design entrepreneurial training for scientists with both “micro” and “macro” issues in mind.

Data Sharing in Hybrid Marketplaces With Endogenous Fee Setting
papers.abstract: We study a hybrid marketplace where a vertically integrated platform competes with a seller, who pays the platform a transaction fee, in a horizontally differentiated downstream market. The platform has a data advantage that allows it to price discriminate against consumers and can choose to share such data with the seller. First, in a setting where the transaction fee is exogenous, we show that the platform may opt to share data with the seller. However, although data sharing increases total welfare, such practice is never Pareto‐improving: in particular, whenever data sharing increases the platform's profits, it also hurts consumers. Second, we show that, if the platform can endogenously choose the transaction fee, it always shares data, as it sets the fee to avoid competition with the seller, leading to higher profits and lower consumer surplus. This result is robust to a large family of consumer distributions. From a policy perspective, we show how a consumer‐oriented policymaker would prefer to ban the practice of price discrimination altogether, as this policy would also level the playing field while simultaneously avoiding the surplus extraction stemming from price discrimination. Finally, we also discuss the welfare consequences of banning the hybrid business model, and we argue that the incentives of the platform to soften downstream competition to increase surplus extraction would remain qualitatively unchanged.
papers.summary: We study a hybrid marketplace where a vertically integrated platform competes with a seller, who pays the platform a transaction fee, in a horizontally differentiated downstream market.

papers.title: Dancing to multiple tunes: Establishing legitimacy with first‐time and repeat backers in crowdfunding campaigns
papers.abstract: Research Summary Using 14,108 Kickstarter crowdfunding campaigns, we examine three strategies to gather support from first‐time versus repeat backers: narrative distinctiveness aligning with backers' expectations of novelty, endorsement from Kickstarter staff, and campaign leadership's reciprocity of funding other campaigns. Staff endorsement is more strongly associated with support from first‐time backers, while campaign leadership's reciprocity is associated primarily with repeat backers. Differences between first‐time and repeat backers are evident in evaluating narrative distinctiveness: narratives distinct from past campaigns correlate positively with repeat backers and greater funding but negatively with first‐time backers. Narratives distinct from live campaigns correlate positively with first‐time backers but are associated with lower funding amounts. Our findings conceptualize differences between first‐time and repeat backers that shape the associations between campaign legitimization strategies and backer support. Managerial Summary This work examines how Kickstarter campaigns should be designed to attract both new people and get support from existing community members. We test whether differences between these two target groups exist in evaluating commonly established “success factors” of campaigns: An endorsement from Kickstarter, the involvement of the campaign founder on the platform, and a campaign text highlighting the campaign's novel contributions. We find differences in all three between both groups and conclude with insights on how managers should design crowdfunding campaigns based on long‐term goals and objectives. We also offer some implications for crowdfunding platforms, such as Kickstarter, in supporting content creators in attracting new backers, which aids with overall platform growth.
papers.summary: Research Summary Using 14,108 Kickstarter crowdfunding campaigns, we examine three strategies to gather support from first‐time versus repeat backers: narrative distinctiveness aligning with backers' expectations of novelty, endorsement from Kickstarter…

papers.title: Micro‐transitions and work identity: The case of academic entrepreneurs
papers.abstract: Research Summary This paper examines how academic entrepreneurs—scientists who found research‐based startups while remaining in academia—construct and sustain their professional identities amid frequent transitions between academic and entrepreneurial roles. Drawing on 27 interviews with Swedish academic entrepreneurs, we show that hybrid identities are not simply the result of reconciling abstract role categories but are shaped through the material and practical organization of everyday work. We introduce the concept of professional micro‐transitions as a key site of identity formation and argue that material artifacts and routines play a central role in this process. This study contributes to the literatures on identity work, role transitions, and academic entrepreneurship by offering a granular, materially grounded account of how hybrid identities are enacted and sustained in practice. Managerial Summary This article investigates how academic entrepreneurs—university scientists who create startups to commercialize research results while remaining in academia—manage to build a hybrid professional identity when frequently switching back and forth between their jobs as academics and for‐profit entrepreneurs. The findings reveal how they creatively find cross‐fertilizing effects between their academic and entrepreneurial work tasks. This in turn allows them to reevaluate and extend their professional identity. For universities, incubators, and policymakers, this study suggests that supporting academic entrepreneurship is not just about funding or IP policies. It also requires recognizing the practical identity work involved and creating flexible environments that allow scientists to integrate both roles in meaningful ways.
papers.summary: Research Summary This paper examines how academic entrepreneurs—scientists who found research‐based startups while remaining in academia—construct and sustain their professional identities amid frequent transitions between academic and entrepreneurial roles.

papers.title: Learning to innovate: How and when firms transform intellectual capital into exploratory and exploitative innovation
papers.abstract: Research Summary Corporate entrepreneurship (CE) requires firms to pursue both exploratory and exploitative innovation, yet limited research explains how intellectual capital (IC) is translated into these distinct outcomes. We develop a contingency model that specifies how and when IC drives exploration and exploitation. We theorize that a firm's capacity for learning and transformation (CLT) functions as a firm‐level learning and transformation capability through which IC can be translated into either exploratory or exploitative innovation. Knowledge breadth strengthens the indirect effect of IC on exploratory innovation via CLT, whereas knowledge depth amplifies the indirect effect on exploitative innovation. We test the model in two complementary field studies. Study 1 employs a time‐lagged design with objective archival data, and Study 2 replicates the findings using survey data. Results consistently support the proposed theoretical model. Managerial Summary Firms operating in fast‐changing and uncertain environments often struggle to balance developing new products with improving existing ones. Our study shows that simply having strong knowledge resources is not enough. What matters is how effectively firms learn from and use that knowledge. We find that firms perform better when they build strong learning capabilities that help them adapt, recombine, and apply knowledge over time. Importantly, the type of knowledge a firm holds shapes this process: broad knowledge supports new product development, while deep, specialized knowledge strengthens improvements to existing products. For managers, this means focusing not only on acquiring knowledge but also on building systems and practices that continuously translate knowledge into action and innovation.
papers.summary: Research Summary Corporate entrepreneurship (CE) requires firms to pursue both exploratory and exploitative innovation, yet limited research explains how intellectual capital (IC) is translated into these distinct outcomes.

papers.title: Paid‐free differentiation in freemium: Understanding the balance between discovery and cannibalization and its implications for paid product sales
papers.abstract: Research Summary Entrepreneurs in digital markets often introduce free versions of their paid products to boost their visibility. This freemium strategy involves a trade‐off between discovery and cannibalization. We study how feature‐based differentiation between the paid product and its free version shapes this trade‐off and its consequences for paid product sales. We theorize that the relationship between paid‐free differentiation and paid product sales is inverted U‐shaped, because moderate levels of paid‐differentiation significantly reduce cannibalization costs while discovery benefits remain largely intact. We further argue that paid‐free differentiation is more salient when the value of the free version is enhanced through network effects, but less so if the free version contains value‐eroding, third‐party advertising. We analyze paid apps from the iOS App Store utilizing the freemium strategy. Managerial Summary Freemium strategies by which entrepreneurs introduce a free product version to boost the discoverability of their paid product have become enormously popular in digital markets. But aside from providing discovery benefits, the free version also cannibalizes the paid product's sales. We investigate whether this trade‐off can be resolved through value‐adding, feature‐based differentiation between the paid product and the free version. Analyzing paid apps from the iOS App Store utilizing the freemium strategy, we find that there is a point of optimal paid‐free differentiation that favors substantial, though not maximal, differentiation. Paid‐free differentiation is especially important when the free version provides more value to consumers by means of network effects. Paid‐free differentiation is less important when the free version contains third‐party advertisements that erode its value.
papers.summary: Research Summary Entrepreneurs in digital markets often introduce free versions of their paid products to boost their visibility. This freemium strategy involves a trade‐off between discovery and cannibalization.

papers.title: From dual-use to omni-use: How firms' strategic responses reproduce institutional lock-in in European technology governance
papers.abstract: Technologies with both civilian and military applications are increasingly boundaryless, yet European technology governance still classifies them through the category of dual-use. This paper asks why the category persists despite its growing misalignment with omni-use technologies, and how the firms governed by it sustain that persistence. Combining institutional isomorphism with Oliver's (1991) strategic responses, and drawing on 32 semi-structured interviews with venture capitalists, policymakers, military officials, prime contractors, entrepreneurs, and scholars, we treat Germany as an extreme case. The findings show that coercive, normative, and mimetic institutional pressures place firms in a dual bind: they must appear civilian to secure civilian capital and pass environmental, social and governance (ESG) screens, yet remain defence-relevant to access defence procurement and public funding. Firms navigate this bind through acquiescence, compromise, and avoidance. Although individually rational, these strategic responses collectively validate the civilian-military separation and withdraw firms from the defence channel, thereby reproducing the category that constrains them. The result is a self-reinforcing institutional lock-in that limits innovation and restricts capital for deep-tech firms. Because the firm-level responses do not alter the institutional conditions that generate the bind, breaking the lock-in requires changes to those conditions by the actors who control them, particularly policymakers.
papers.summary: Technologies with both civilian and military applications are increasingly boundaryless, yet European technology governance still classifies them through the category of dual-use.

papers.title: Human Capital as a Driver of Automation: Theory and Evidence From China's College Expansion
papers.abstract: This paper studies how human capital shapes both the level and direction of automation. We develop an endogenous Schumpeterian growth model in which skilled labor is allocated across production, horizontal automation of new tasks, and vertical upgrading of existing automated tasks. A positive skilled‐labor shock reallocates labor toward R&D and accelerates automation along both margins. Using China's 1999 college enrollment expansion as a natural experiment, we find that firms in skill‐intensive industries increased robot adoption significantly more after the reform, with a stronger effect on the horizontal than the vertical margin.
papers.summary: This paper studies how human capital shapes both the level and direction of automation.

papers.title: The coevolution of trust and behavioral uncertainty: Toward a theory of vulnerability acceptance in entrepreneurial ventures
papers.abstract: Research Summary This conceptual study develops a process theory of vulnerability acceptance explaining how trust and behavioral uncertainty coevolve as entrepreneurial actors form, interpret, and realize opportunities. Trust is frequently invoked to explain creativity, exploration, and opportunity formation, yet remains theorized through predictability and evaluability, which entrepreneurial opportunities often lack ex ante. We distinguish three forms of vulnerability acceptance: uncertainty creating, releasing, and decreasing trust. Each transforms the uncertainty it engages, which in turn reinforces or unsettles that form, so no form is terminal. Their salience shifts across opportunity formation, interpretive recombination, and realization, and misalignment between a form and the conditions it confronts impairs entrepreneurial progress. Trust thereby becomes a means through which epistemic conditions are produced, not only a response to them. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurship exposes forms of vulnerability that cannot be explained by risk‐based models of trust alone. Entrepreneurs often face the practical question: “Trust them to do what?” The answer depends on the kind of agency they are willing to be vulnerable to, and it changes as an opportunity takes shape. That may mean backing people to take the work somewhere no one can yet specify, relying on others' expertise to make sense of what is emerging, or counting on them to deliver what was agreed. Trust is therefore not only a way of reducing uncertainty but a means of transforming it, and progress depends on recognizing when the prevailing form fits the conditions and when it does not.
papers.summary: Research Summary This conceptual study develops a process theory of vulnerability acceptance explaining how trust and behavioral uncertainty coevolve as entrepreneurial actors form, interpret, and realize opportunities.

papers.title: Academic entrepreneurs' material engagements in the creation of science‐based ventures
papers.abstract: Research Summary This paper examines the creation of entrepreneurial opportunities under coupled technical and demand uncertainty within science‐based ventures (SBVs). Whereas opportunity creation theory emphasizes discursive processes, we build on practice theory and pragmatism to explore how SBV opportunities also emerge through entrepreneurs' evolving engagements with indeterminate material artifacts. Through a longitudinal multiple‐case study, we identify two patterns of material engagement: epistemic engagement, oriented toward knowledge creation, and pragmatic engagement, oriented toward practical use. We show how opportunity creation unfolds through interweaving cycles of epistemic and pragmatic engagement. By introducing material engagements as constitutive, we specify creation theory for SBVs and highlight the central role of materiality in shaping belief formation, opportunity objectification, stakeholder engagement, and the variation–selection–retention process. Managerial Summary This paper explores how entrepreneurs create science‐based ventures (SBVs) by engaging with evolving material artifacts, like sensors and prototypes. Based on a study of SBV initiatives supported by the European Commission's ATTRACT program, we identify a process in which entrepreneurs repeatedly alternate between epistemic engagement—focused on scientific understanding—and pragmatic engagement—focused on usability and implementation. This material engagement cycle plays a central role in venture development under coupled technical and demand uncertainty. We highlight tensions inherent in this process and the strategies through which they are accommodated, offering practical insights for entrepreneurs building ventures from frontier science and policymakers supporting science commercialization.
papers.summary: Research Summary This paper examines the creation of entrepreneurial opportunities under coupled technical and demand uncertainty within science‐based ventures (SBVs).

papers.title: How ventures maintain stakeholder support amidst operational legitimacy threats
papers.abstract: Research Summary We explore how ventures mitigate operational legitimacy threats—threats that originate within the venture and challenge claims relating to the venture's ability to deliver on its promised value proposition. Through an inductive study of four ventures working to deliver their promised products following successful crowdfunding campaigns, we reveal a process of three rhetorical practices that ventures can use to maintain stakeholder support: humanizing the venture, normalizing setbacks and resolutions, and revising pragmatic claims. The first two practices contribute to the formation of dispositional legitimacy buffers that allow the third practice to be effective in mitigating fallout from exposed operational legitimacy threats. We conclude by offering contributions to the cultural entrepreneurship literature and to research on venture–stakeholder communication. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs must often determine whether to disclose operational issues to stakeholders. On one hand, entrepreneurs may resolve these operational issues without stakeholders ever knowing of their occurrence. On the other hand, such issues could balloon to negatively impact whether a venture can deliver its promised offering. We identify three rhetorical practices, two of which entrepreneurs can utilize before an operational issue even occurs, to generate favorable judgments with stakeholders and increase the likelihood that their ventures will be able to maintain support if an operational issue becomes exposed.
papers.summary: Research Summary We explore how ventures mitigate operational legitimacy threats—threats that originate within the venture and challenge claims relating to the venture's ability to deliver on its promised value proposition.

papers.title: Logical reframing: A theory‐based view of entrepreneurial persuasion
papers.abstract: Research Summary Prior literature that addresses how entrepreneurs systematically deal with Knightian uncertainty has primarily focused on individual entrepreneurs but has largely neglected that, to be successful, entrepreneurs must also persuade others of their view of the future. Uncertainty implies that others may initially have different and potentially conflicting framings of the future. In this article we offer a belief revision framework for persuasion under uncertainty based on the idea of logical reframing: using and communicating theories and what‐if beliefs that allow recipients to draw logical conclusions in line with the sender's view. Our propositions identify the trade‐offs the receiver has to make between contradictory explanations in her mind so she can be persuaded. The central insight from our framework concerns the role of filters, which are sets of beliefs that create resistance against an argument. Overall, our article contributes by taking the theory‐based view of entrepreneurship to a multi‐agent setting. We also continue the formalization of the theory‐based view, introducing ranking theory, which can be used to model how agents revise their beliefs, to the management literature. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs often need stakeholders to accept not only a proposed action but also a shared account of why that action can succeed under uncertainty. We develop a framework of logical reframing in which entrepreneurs use arguments to connect stakeholders’ existing beliefs to a desired conclusion. Persuasion requires a complete logical route to that conclusion, a theory whose weakest premise is sufficiently strong and can overcome any additional contradictions activated by the argument. We show that what‐if beliefs can prepare stakeholders to accept an argument but they can also generate resistance by connecting the argument to conflicting prior beliefs. papers.summary: Research Summary Prior literature that addresses how entrepreneurs systematically deal with Knightian uncertainty has primarily focused on individual entrepreneurs but has largely neglected that, to be successful, entrepreneurs must also persuade others of their view of the future.

papers.title: Multidimensional mechanism design and robust revenue maximization in multi-object auctions
All-pay quality-bids in score procurement auctions
Orchestrating the Distributive Process: Baron and Ferejohn Meet Tullock
Sequential Non-Bayesian Persuasion
Poverty traps under endogenous discounting
Industrialization, class conflict, and the closing window of democratic opportunity
papers.abstract: This paper addresses two long-standing questions in the political economy of development: how the timing of industrialization affects the transition to democracy and how different social classes shape that transition. We develop a sequential game among landed elites, industrialists, and workers embedded in a growth model with endogenous industrialization. The model identifies a window of democratic opportunity during which the industrial class prefers democracy to industrial autocracy. Whether democracy occurs depends on two dimensions of workers’ de facto political power: their power against the landed class determines when industrialization occurs and when landed rule ends; their power against the industrial class determines when the democratic window closes. Later industrialization therefore makes democratization less likely but not impossible. A calibration to Great Britain and numerical exercises for early and late industrializers show that the revolt threat required to sustain democracy rises as industrialization is delayed. Faster technological growth advances political transitions but does not, by itself, determine whether democracy or industrial autocracy follows landed rule.
papers.summary: This paper addresses two long-standing questions in the political economy of development: how the timing of industrialization affects the transition to democracy and how different social classes shape that transition.

papers.title: Carbon emissions regulation, input-output networks, and firm dynamics: The case of a low-carbon-zone pilot in China
papers.abstract: Input-output linkages among sectors and firms are largely overlooked when assessing regulatory policies. Using a carbon emissions regulation in China as an example, we find that the regulation facilitates the transition to green technologies and reduces entry and carbon emissions in the regulated sectors with large carbon emissions. We also find unintended spillovers via the input-output network, resulting in more entry and innovation in the downstream sectors; and less entry and innovation in the upstream sectors. These facts can be rationalized by a firm-dynamics model with input-output linkages. The results of quantitative exercises are substantially different when taking input-output linkages into account.
papers.summary: Input-output linkages among sectors and firms are largely overlooked when assessing regulatory policies.

papers.title: Happy Pills? The Health Consequences of the Dramatic Increase in Antidepressant Use
papers.abstract: This paper examines the health consequences of the rapid increase in antidepressant consumption in Switzerland (2002–2014). Using a shift-share instrumental variable approach, we exploit regional variation in sales driven by product innovation (the shift) and the market power of pharmaceutical firms (the share). Our findings reveal that a one defined daily dose per 1,000 inhabitants increase in antidepressant sales raises hospital admissions for adverse drug reactions by 18% and for depression by 6%. Financial incentives for self-dispensing doctors and reduced access to psychotherapy emerge as key drivers, highlighting concerns about overtreatment and suboptimal prescribing practices.
papers.summary: This paper examines the health consequences of the rapid increase in antidepressant consumption in Switzerland (2002–2014).

papers.title: Large language models and economic history: A comment on Ferrara (2026)
Quantifying undetected severe misconduct in medical research
Understanding multi-level dynamics in rural entrepreneurial ecosystems: A conceptual framework and research agenda
papers.abstract: Rural regions occupy vast territories and often exhibit spatial dispersion, limited institutional support, constrained resources, and scarce market opportunities. Yet entrepreneurial activity develops under these conditions. This coexistence creates a theoretical puzzle for entrepreneurial ecosystem (EE) research, as rural EE operate despite several conditions commonly associated with effective ecosystem functioning being comparatively weak or dispersed. We conduct a bibliometric–systematic review of 71 articles on rural EE, identifying four thematic clusters and synthesizing them into a multi-level conceptual framework and eight research propositions. Grounded in complex adaptive systems theory and informed by a multi-level mechanisms perspective, we conceptualize rural EE as compensatory cross-level systems operating under conditions of structural thinness. We theorize that structural thinness changes the functional logic of EE as available ecosystem elements assume broader, more interdependent, and compensatory roles. Whereas denser EE, often associated with urban environments, may rely comparatively more on abundant and specialized ecosystem elements, rural EE functioning becomes relatively more dependent on adaptive alignment. We conceptualize adaptive alignment as an emergent system-level mechanism through which ecosystem elements continually adjust their roles and relationships via recurring processes of coordination, feedback, resource recombination, and mutual adjustment across analytical levels. Adaptive alignment sustains rural EE functioning, thereby supporting entrepreneurial activity and shaping regional value creation. By theorizing that structural thinness changes not merely the availability of ecosystem elements but the functional logic through which they become connected and collectively sustain ecosystem functioning, we extend the boundary conditions of prevailing EE explanations and inform more context-sensitive research, policy, and practice in
papers.summary: Rural regions occupy vast territories and often exhibit spatial dispersion, limited institutional support, constrained resources, and scarce market opportunities. Yet entrepreneurial activity develops under these conditions.

papers.title: Monopoly Versus Dual‐Channel Distribution With Multiple Retailers
papers.abstract: This paper examines how downstream competition shapes a manufacturer's decision to adopt a dual‐channel structure—supplying independent retailers via secret two‐part tariff contracts while also operating a direct channel. We show that the shape of the inverse demand function plays a key role in this decision. Under strictly concave demand, expanding total output raises price sensitivity, while the manufacturer responds less aggressively through its direct channel. These effects lead to a sharp price drop, discouraging aggressive retailer behavior and favoring a dual‐channel structure. In contrast, under strictly convex demand, output expansion reduces price sensitivity, and the manufacturer retreats aggressively. The resulting mild price decline leads each retailer to believe that its own output increase has little market impact, encouraging aggressive competition. As a result, with multiple retailers, the manufacturer may avoid supplying the indirect channel even when only two retailers are present. We further show that under the dual‐channel structure, a higher direct‐channel cost can increase consumer surplus by overly shifting output toward the more efficient indirect channel.
papers.summary: This paper examines how downstream competition shapes a manufacturer's decision to adopt a dual‐channel structure—supplying independent retailers via secret two‐part tariff contracts while also operating a direct channel.

papers.title: Opening Hours and Consumer Behavior: Evidence From GPS Data and Deregulation
papers.abstract: In 2019, North Dakota repealed its Sunday closing law, which had required most non‐grocery stores to close between midnight and noon. Using this policy change and consumer GPS data, we study the impact of opening hours on shopping behavior and welfare. We compare visits before and after the repeal in North Dakota and neighboring states using difference‐in‐differences and event‐study designs. The repeal caused a large increase in Sunday morning visits, originating partly from intertemporal, store‐type, and cross‐border substitution. The closing law's welfare loss is equivalent to increasing the travel distance to affected stores by about 1.4 miles per consumer.
papers.summary: In 2019, North Dakota repealed its Sunday closing law, which had required most non‐grocery stores to close between midnight and noon. Using this policy change and consumer GPS data, we study the impact of opening hours on shopping behavior and welfare.

papers.title: Life‐Cycle Wage Growth and Firm Productivity in Developed and Developing Economies
papers.abstract: Life‐cycle wage growth varies substantially across countries. We study the firm productivity distribution's role in a random‐search model with learning and labor‐market frictions, estimated for Brazil, Colombia, and the United States. Brazil has a long left tail of low‐paying firms, and Colombia has a highly compressed firm ladder. Replacing each country's firm distribution with that of the United States closes most of the cross‐country gap in wage growth, raising Brazil's relative wage growth from 73 to 103 percent and Colombia's from 52 to 115 percent. The results are robust to alternative distributional assumptions and additional sensitivity checks.
papers.summary: Life‐cycle wage growth varies substantially across countries. We study the firm productivity distribution's role in a random‐search model with learning and labor‐market frictions, estimated for Brazil, Colombia, and the United States.

papers.title: Information Aggregation With Delegation of Votes
papers.abstract: Liquid democracy (LD) combines elements of direct and representative democracy: voters can either vote directly or delegate their votes to others. We study its information aggregation properties in a setting with heterogeneously and privately informed independent and partisan voters. We establish that LD always has equilibria that improve welfare and information aggregation relative to direct democracy, identify economically interpretable conditions under which these gains are strict, and characterise optimal delegation for salient classes of committees. However, while delegation improves the best‐equilibrium, it can also introduce robust inefficient equilibria that perform worse than direct democracy.
papers.summary: Liquid democracy (LD) combines elements of direct and representative democracy: voters can either vote directly or delegate their votes to others.

papers.title: Growing Pains: Inefficient Resource Allocation in Emerging Economies
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how economic catch‐up shapes resource allocation in emerging economies. I develop a model that features firm‐specific technology adoption and costly adjustment of production factors. Rapid technological progress during catch‐up creates strong demand for reallocating resources from slow to fast adopters, amplifying the consequences of adjustment costs. The amplification fades as technological change gradually slows during convergence to a more advanced and efficient steady state. I evaluate the model using Chinese and German enterprise data and find that differences in development stage account for at least 40% of their labour allocative efficiency gap.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how economic catch‐up shapes resource allocation in emerging economies. I develop a model that features firm‐specific technology adoption and costly adjustment of production factors.

papers.title: Place‐Based Land Policy and Spatial Misallocation: Theory and Evidence From China
papers.abstract: We investigate a land policy in China that allocated more urban land quotas to underdeveloped regions to reduce regional gaps. Empirically, the policy decreased productivity in eastern areas relative to the inland.
