A spatial equilibrium model with migration, land quota constraints, and agglomeration shows the policy distorts labor and production across regions, causing substantial output losses. Though regional gaps narrowed, workers from underdeveloped areas migrated less and earned less. Without the policy, national output would have been 1.8% higher, and workers in underdeveloped areas would have earned 1.6% more in 2010. Regional transfers offer a less distortionary alternative for reducing inequality.
papers.summary: We investigate a land policy in China that allocated more urban land quotas to underdeveloped regions to reduce regional gaps. Empirically, the policy decreased productivity in eastern areas relative to the inland.

papers.title: From critique to catalyst: How academic entrepreneurs transform negative feedback into pivots and performance
papers.abstract: Research Summary This study examines how academic entrepreneurs refine business ideas in response to external critique and how these responses relate to performance. We develop a framework that links feedback (critique), business‐idea changes (pivots), and performance, and test it using detailed data on external stakeholder feedback, changes to the business idea's core and periphery, and commercialization outcomes in 316 academic‐led teams. We find that academic entrepreneurs frequently modify their business idea's core in response to negative feedback, and that core changes—rather than peripheral ones—are positively associated with commercialization. Challenging the idea that all entrepreneurs are inertial, we find that academic entrepreneurs both actively embrace and benefit from changes to the business idea's core. By tracing the feedback‐response dynamics of business idea components, our study adds granularity to research on pivoting. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs often face a choice between reworking the core of a business idea and making changes to its periphery. Analyzing 316 academic‐led teams seeking to commercialize technologies using the Lean Startup Method, we find that academic‐led teams frequently change their idea's core in response to negative feedback—and that only core changes, rather than peripheral changes, are linked to improved commercialization outcomes. Overall, the results show the effectiveness of the Lean Startup Method and demonstrate that focusing feedback on the core of the business idea is an effective way to provide feedback to academic entrepreneurs.
papers.summary: Research Summary This study examines how academic entrepreneurs refine business ideas in response to external critique and how these responses relate to performance.

papers.title: The signal of institutional governance in early‐stage financing for university spinoffs
papers.abstract: Research Summary University spinoffs (USOs) translate scientific advancement to economic gains, but the role of the university's governance as a public or private institution is infrequently explored. With a novel dataset of academic entrepreneurs with National Science Foundation I‐Corps training, we examine institutional governance as a fundraising signal. We demonstrate how angel investors and venture capitalists (VCs) show a preference for private USOs. However, with different investment objectives, the groups conduct distinct sensemaking that weighs this cue differently. For angels, industry moderates the effect such that they prefer private university life science firms to public USOs. However, industry mediates the effect for VCs, who prefer life sciences to engineering. We describe this variation as mixed salience—when a signal yields differences in decision‐making for distinct audiences. Managerial Summary University spinoffs (USOs) are important for economic growth, but little is known about differences between USOs from public and private universities. We study how angel investors and venture capitalists (VCs) fund USOs of public and private schools. These two investor groups make funding decisions with different priorities and approaches. Both groups appear to prefer private universities. A deeper look reveals that angel investors prefer private university life science teams to the public university counterparts. On the other hand, VCs prefer life sciences teams to engineering teams—and life sciences teams are more likely to come from private schools. Evidently, the two investor audiences respond to the public/private distinction in different ways.
papers.summary: Research Summary University spinoffs (USOs) translate scientific advancement to economic gains, but the role of the university's governance as a public or private institution is infrequently explored.

papers.title: Accounting for the Evolution of China's Production and Trade Patterns
papers.abstract: We study the evolution of China's production and trade patterns during its integration into the global economy. Using firm‐level microdata, we document how production and exports shifted across industries and within industries across firms. We quantify a Ricardian–Heckscher–Ohlin model with heterogeneous firms to account for these changes. Counterfactuals show capital deepening pushed China's production and exports toward greater capital intensity, while labor‐biased productivity growth provided an offsetting force. The model generates an inverted‐U pattern in China's trade openness—peaking in the mid‐2000s and declining through the 2020s—alongside a continuous rise in the world's exposure to Chinese exports.
papers.summary: We study the evolution of China's production and trade patterns during its integration into the global economy. Using firm‐level microdata, we document how production and exports shifted across industries and within industries across firms.

papers.title: Asset Market Participation, Redistribution, and Asset Pricing
papers.abstract: We study how redistribution between asset holders and non‐asset holders links macroeconomic fluctuations to expected stock returns. Aggregate and relative consumption growth forecast excess returns with opposite signs and at different horizons. We interpret these patterns using a production‐based asset‐pricing model with limited participation and external habits. Aggregate (relative) consumption captures variation in the price (quantity) of risk. Technology shocks drive macroeconomic fluctuations, whereas redistributive shocks generate large short‐run movements in inequality and are the main source of priced risk. This points to a macro‐finance disconnect between the drivers of business cycles and those governing risk premia.
papers.summary: We study how redistribution between asset holders and non‐asset holders links macroeconomic fluctuations to expected stock returns. Aggregate and relative consumption growth forecast excess returns with opposite signs and at different horizons.

papers.title: Multi‐Agent Contracting With Network Externalities
papers.abstract: ABSTRACTThis paper analyzes how the structure of externalities‐encompassing both pure spillovers and interactive components‐reshapes the classic trade‐off between incentives and risk in multi‐agent contracts. The interplay of network effects and moral hazard generates congestion effects among agents with a common neighbor, which we decompose into a sum of weighted Katz‐Bonacich centralities. This tractable characterization enables clear comparative statics on the externality structure. We further apply the framework to examine how organization structures shape firm boundaries, and the design of Pigovian taxes to generate social security.
papers.summary: ABSTRACTThis paper analyzes how the structure of externalities‐encompassing both pure spillovers and interactive components‐reshapes the classic trade‐off between incentives and risk in multi‐agent contracts.

papers.title: The Dynamics of the Racial Wealth Gap
papers.abstract: We study the dynamics of the racial wealth gap (the wealth of Black households relative to white ones) using a dynamic equilibrium model of overlapping generations. We match the model to the cross‐sectional distributions of wealth and earnings by race. We find that equalizing earnings is critical for permanent reductions in racial wealth inequality, and that one‐time transfers will have only transitory effects unless earnings are also equalized. Our results are robust to the introduction of racial differences in returns to saving, which only matter after earnings inequality is reduced.
papers.summary: We study the dynamics of the racial wealth gap (the wealth of Black households relative to white ones) using a dynamic equilibrium model of overlapping generations. We match the model to the cross‐sectional distributions of wealth and earnings by race.

papers.title: The Decentralization of Liquor Policies in Texas During the Post‐Prohibition Era
papers.abstract: We examine the decentralization of liquor policies in Texas during the Post‐Prohibition era using newly collected historical legislative roll call data. By combining these data with local referendum vote shares, we analyze both legislators' and constituents' preferences on liquor policy. We develop a probabilistic voting model incorporating spillovers and peer effects. Results reveal substantial heterogeneity in preferences among voters, reflecting differing attitudes toward alcohol regulation. Spillover effects are significant, yet the model predicts notable gains from decentralization. Finally, we link legislators' policy preferences to alcohol consumption data and compare model‐based welfare estimates with traditional consumption‐based measures.
papers.summary: We examine the decentralization of liquor policies in Texas during the Post‐Prohibition era using newly collected historical legislative roll call data.

papers.title: Value Created, Value Leaked: Shareholder Activism and Employee-Initiated Data Leaks
papers.abstract: Financially motivated shareholder activism is a well-established mechanism for enhancing shareholder value, improving governance, and driving operational efficiency. Yet as activism reshapes corporate priorities, relatively little is known about how retained employees interpret and respond to these changes. Grounded in organizational justice theory, we propose that activist campaigns may shift some employees’ perceptions of distributive justice—altering the perceived balance between what they contribute and what they receive—in ways that increase the likelihood of employee-initiated data leaks. These behavioral responses, which range from deliberate disclosure driven by frustration to lapses in vigilance under pressure, are concentrated among the demands employees experience as most consequential to their daily work. Importantly, however, firms can mitigate these risks: strong track records of employee-oriented corporate social responsibility and high preexisting employee satisfaction buffer the relationship between shareholder activism and data leaks. Using difference-in-differences estimation with a novel dataset of employee-initiated data leaks, we find support for these relationships. Our findings illuminate an overlooked employee dimension of shareholder activism, showing how campaigns may inadvertently elevate internal information risk—and what firms can do to guard against it.
papers.summary: Financially motivated shareholder activism is a well-established mechanism for enhancing shareholder value, improving governance, and driving operational efficiency.

papers.title: Agricultural Trade and Industrial Development
papers.abstract: Is agricultural productivity conducive to economic development? We develop a two‐country open‐economy Schumpeterian growth model with endogenous takeoff. With both agricultural trade and a subsistence requirement, higher domestic agricultural productivity has ambiguous effects on the economy's takeoff and its transitional growth rate if domestic and imported agricultural goods are substitutes. Without the subsistence requirement, higher domestic agricultural productivity delays industrialization and lowers transitional growth by increasing domestic demand for agricultural labor. This specialization force works in the opposite direction of the change in domestic consumption pattern governed by the subsistence requirement, which tends to release labor from agriculture. Without agricultural trade, the specialization force is absent and the subsistence requirement on agricultural consumption implies that higher domestic agricultural productivity reallocates labor from agriculture to industry, hastening industrialization and raising transitional growth. Using cross‐country panel data, we find that agricultural productivity has a positive effect on economic growth but this positive effect weakens and even becomes negative when reliance on agricultural imports is sufficiently high. Simulating the calibrated model, we find that improvement in domestic agricultural productivity accounts for about 30% and 15% of the changes in TFP growth in China and Japan, respectively, and more so for their main trading partner, the United States.
papers.summary: Is agricultural productivity conducive to economic development? We develop a two‐country open‐economy Schumpeterian growth model with endogenous takeoff.

papers.title: Rational Expectations Fools' Bubbles
papers.abstract: We develop a rational, Walrasian model of speculative bubbles inspired by the Kindleberger–Minsky view, which describes bubbles as wave‐like market processes. Touched off by an initial shock, price booms are initially self‐reinforcing but become self‐destructive later when prices surpass fundamental value. Previous models in this vein have been criticized due to ad hoc features, such as prices driven by behavioral forces or particular trading protocols. Our model allays these concerns by relying only on multidimensional uncertainty to prevent unraveling via backward induction. Standard market clearing, moreover, makes the model more compatible with established macroeconomic and asset pricing frameworks.
papers.summary: We develop a rational, Walrasian model of speculative bubbles inspired by the Kindleberger–Minsky view, which describes bubbles as wave‐like market processes.

papers.title: The Interaction Between Credit and Labor Market Frictions
papers.abstract: I study a novel two‐way feedback between credit and labor market frictions. Running from credit to labor markets, amplitude in capital demand caused by collateral constraints spills over onto labor demand due to the complementarity of capital and labor; and, furthermore, credit frictions raise effective financial hiring costs, prompting firms to delay hiring in recessions. Running back from labor to credit markets, search frictions imply that wages move less than one‐to‐one with productivity; this induces greater volatility of net worth, via the wage bill, which then spills over onto capital demand. Together, these considerably amplify labor and capital market dynamics.
papers.summary: I study a novel two‐way feedback between credit and labor market frictions.

papers.title: Immigration and child mortality during the Age of Mass Migration
1918 Influenza pandemic across America - New evidence using county-level data
Tilting at Windmills: Evidence on Momentum and Hot Hands
papers.abstract: Successes and failures often appear to propagate. According to one common belief, the experience of winning or losing can alter the cognitive and emotional state of performers, generating a psychological momentum that helps or harms subsequent performance. This belief is often used to rationalize the so-called hot-hand phenomenon, and has been applied to contexts ranging from horseshoe pitching to stock market trading. However, the existence of a causal effect of winning on subsequent performance remains debated. I test whether wins cause more wins (and losses more losses) using a large natural experiment involving almost a quarter billion online chess games. I find that performance is serially correlated, consistent with the existence of hot hands. Surprisingly, however, I find no evidence of causal effects. Players that were given a small random advantage in one game have no advantage in the next. The null effect is precisely estimated, providing credible evidence against the hypothesis that success breeds success in online chess.
papers.summary: Successes and failures often appear to propagate. According to one common belief, the experience of winning or losing can alter the cognitive and emotional state of performers, generating a psychological momentum that helps or harms subsequent performance.

papers.title: The Short and the Long of It: Stock‐Flow Matching in the US Housing Market
papers.abstract: From 2006 until 2020, the probability of selling a house in the U.S. declined sharply after listing for 2 weeks. Moreover, sales within the first 2 weeks of listing (“quick sales”) and sales happening afterward (“slow sales”) behaved differently over the housing cycle. The probability and associated price of a quick sale recovered from the slump sooner, faster, and more prominently than a slow sale. This paper demonstrates that a calibrated stock‐flow matching model not only generates quantitatively consistent sales, prices, listings, and time on the market but also captures distinctions between fast and slow sales over the housing cycle.
papers.summary: From 2006 until 2020, the probability of selling a house in the U.S. declined sharply after listing for 2 weeks.

papers.title: How Does Progressivity Affect the Tax Cut Multiplier?
papers.abstract: How does the targeting of personal income tax cuts affect the output multiplier? This paper provides quantitative evidence using a heterogeneous‐agent New‐Keynesian model calibrated to match US distributions of income, wealth, marginal tax rates, and marginal propensities to consume. Labor supply is determined by household preferences on the intensive margin and search frictions on the extensive margin. The model evaluates tax cuts for the bottom‐90 (B90%) and top‐10% of the income distribution in national and cross‐region settings, replicating influential empirical research designs. B90 tax cuts generate larger output effects while incentive effects play a central role in transmission.
papers.summary: How does the targeting of personal income tax cuts affect the output multiplier?

papers.title: AI and the Two Margins of Work: Why Job Losses Show Up Before Job Creation
papers.abstract: Technological change acts on labor demand at two margins: adjustment within established activities and the creation of additional activities, often by new firms. Payroll statistics record the first promptly and the second late. In the computing era, firms that entered in 1978 or later held 42 percent of payroll by 1998 and entering cohorts kept about 80 percent of their payroll after five years; in the industries most exposed to automation, incumbents contracted before entrants accumulated, a sequence that is precise early in the period and suggestive by its end. We develop a model in which one AI capability lowers the full cost of acceptable output in existing production and makes additional projects worth attempting, with founder effort separate from hired hours. If operating products re-scale instantly, automation displaces no aggregate hours; if they take time, hours fall first and recover as incumbents re-expand and new products arrive, with the long-run sign set by income effects. Establishment job flows through the first quarter of 2026 show no gradient on language-model exposure on either margin, which is what the model predicts under the observed adoption path and also what no effect on payroll would look like; studies with founding-task exposure find entry rising 10 to 20 percent. We propose a net reinstatement ratio and show that statistics which record new work late overstate displacement for years.
papers.summary: Technological change acts on labor demand at two margins: adjustment within established activities and the creation of additional activities, often by new firms. Payroll statistics record the first promptly and the second late.

papers.title: Automating inequality? Gender bias in AI-mediated labor markets
papers.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly entering labor markets, with large language models (LLMs) now used to help write CVs and evaluate applicants. We study the risks this creates in a series of audit experiments in which applicant gender is randomly assigned while all other information is held constant. We find that LLMs generate gender-stereotypical CVs and exhibit gender bias in screening scores and wage recommendations. Screening scores track occupational gender segregation, penalizing women in male-dominated occupations and favoring them in female-dominated ones. Wage recommendations track occupational gender wage gaps when gender is explicit in the prompt, though this gradient weakens under name-based gender signaling and is sensitive to the LLMs being used. These disparities arise through two channels: evaluation bias, when identical CV content is evaluated differently by gender, and generation bias, when gendered content produced by the model affects later evaluation. Because the same systems shape both CV content and its subsequent assessment, these channels can reinforce one another. Taken together, our findings identify measurable risks of algorithmic amplification in AI-mediated job search.
papers.summary: Generative AI is rapidly entering labor markets, with large language models (LLMs) now used to help write CVs and evaluate applicants.

papers.title: Spreads Don't Price a Rival Market Maker's Information
papers.abstract: When one market maker becomes better informed, do its competitors widen their bid-ask spreads? Adverse-selection reasoning suggests that they should, because the better-informed maker avoids toxic order flow and leaves more of it to the others, and the closest model of competition with an informed dealer predicts more conservative quotes by the uninformed dealers. We study this question in a stochastic quoting game in which one maker receives a private signal of varying precision about a persistent state that drives order flow. Strategies are learned with independent reinforcement learning, which we benchmark against an exact dynamic-programming solution of the single-agent case. In none of the configurations we examine does the average spread of the uninformed makers increase with the rival's precision. Where competition for order flow is weak, the slope of their spread in precision is statistically equivalent to zero within half an action tick; where competition is strong, their spread tightens. The informed maker's own spread tightens markedly in every configuration and serves as a positive control. These results hold with two, three and four makers, across an eightfold variation in the depth of the background liquidity, with a background quote that reprices after toxic fills, and under price-time priority. Our measurements point to a competitive trade-off. In the model the total toxicity of the flow does not depend on any maker's information. A better-informed maker avoids more of it, and where this leaves more toxic flow to its competitors, it also quotes more tightly, so that a wider quote would cost them more order flow than it would save in adverse selection. The uninformed makers adjust the skew of their quotes and their inventory instead, and the rival's information changes the distribution of profits across makers while quoted spreads remain nearly unchanged.
papers.summary: When one market maker becomes better informed, do its competitors widen their bid-ask spreads?

papers.title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
papers.abstract: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.
papers.summary: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game.

papers.title: The Geoengineering Put: Ecological Debt, Termination Risk, and Asset Prices
papers.abstract: Solar geoengineering offers an inexpensive and fast-acting way to lower global temperatures without removing carbon from the atmosphere. As warming intensifies, climate-vulnerable countries face growing incentives to deploy geoengineering unilaterally. The economic and financial consequences of this prospect remain largely overlooked. We develop a general equilibrium macro-finance framework in which geoengineering acts as a put option on climate damages, funded by the "ecological debt" of masked warming. If deployment stops, temperatures snap back in a catastrophic termination shock. Anticipation of geoengineering raises current brown firm valuations and lowers the optimal carbon tax, helping explain two puzzles in the existing literature: high brown-firm valuations and low carbon taxes. As ecological debt grows, however, termination risk transforms brown firms into toxic assets. Geoengineering also reshapes green innovation: it buys time for a breakthrough, but can weaken innovation incentives by lowering energy and carbon prices. Termination risk partly restores research incentives and directs them toward carbon removal, which can retire ecological debt. Our calibrations show that the geoengineering put can raise welfare across a range of parameter assumptions. Our framework clarifies how this conclusion depends on uncertain parameters and where further research is most needed.
papers.summary: Solar geoengineering offers an inexpensive and fast-acting way to lower global temperatures without removing carbon from the atmosphere. As warming intensifies, climate-vulnerable countries face growing incentives to deploy geoengineering unilaterally.

papers.title: The opposing informational effects of AI trading
papers.abstract: Better artificial intelligence (AI) can improve individual forecasts without making prices better at revealing new information. In a competitive market with resource-constrained forecasting, more capable algorithms can substitute analysis of public records for private observations, reducing the private information aggregated into prices. The same trades can convey sophisticated public-data analysis to investors unable to perform it themselves. We establish conditions under which these effects coexist and the private benefit of further computation falls. Numerical equilibrium calculations and finite-data neural-market experiments exhibit corresponding patterns. Out-of-sample earnings forecasts and controlled language-model tasks show related patterns of information substitution. In the neural experiment, wider adoption increases the predictive value of price for limited observers, reduces it for advanced observers, and lowers the benefit of upgrading by 44\%. Retraining by investors who did not upgrade can amplify the loss of private-information precision. The informational consequences of AI trading depend on what prices reveal and who can use them.
papers.summary: Better artificial intelligence (AI) can improve individual forecasts without making prices better at revealing new information.

papers.title: Regime-Uncertain Data Transactions: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Self-Adapting and Self-Diagnosing Multi-ML-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Large firms use autonomous machine learning agents that communicate with each other across legal and geographic boundaries. The rules governing a particular transfer are fluid. They depend on where the data subject lives, where the agents operate, who their owners and targets are, and how many different versions of the rules are in effect. Descriptions of the data using tags can be inaccurate, and the counterpart agent may exaggerate its security measures.We model such a transaction between two ML agents as a regime-uncertain transfer game, with a third player acting as the enforcer. The set of rules is represented as hard constraints with a strictest-wins logic. Both agents maintain Bayesian beliefs about which rules apply. They can spend money to gain access to security measures and verify the counterpart's claims, and then negotiate within the remaining legal space using Legally-Constrained Nash Bargaining (LCNB).Using the Monotonic Concession Protocol with Zeuthen's rule, we design LCNB. We prove four properties of the model and implement it in a simulated setting with GDPR, DPDP, CCPA/CPRA, and a fictional stricter regime.Across three stress tests where residence and citizenship are at odds, the citizenship-based rule is violated in 21 to 37 percent of shared data records, while LCNB results in a violation rate of less than 1 percent.There are limitations to our results. With our default economics, LCNB shares virtually all aggregates, while having a low rate of violations partly due to this.
papers.summary: Large firms use autonomous machine learning agents that communicate with each other across legal and geographic boundaries. The rules governing a particular transfer are fluid.

papers.title: Payoff-Based Certificates for Convergence to Pure Nash Equilibria under Replicator Dynamics
papers.abstract: For finite bimatrix games, we give a payoff-based sufficient condition $E>0$ for an interior initial state to converge to a specified strict pure Nash equilibrium under replicator dynamics. The construction combines lower bounds on the growth rates of log probability ratios between target and alternative actions with a first integral of a two-dimensional comparison system. It allows one player's payoff advantage to compensate for the other's disadvantage, certifying convergence even when a target action initially loses probability. For rational inputs and integration base points with algebraic exponentials, we give a finite exact test. We obtain closed-form box probabilities and, when all nontarget actions are included, closed-form upper bounds on convergence time. In two-action coordination games, choosing the base points at the sign thresholds recovers the full basin of attraction. Experiments on random games show that basin coverage shrinks rapidly with the number of actions. For $n=4,5,6$, median entry times are approximately 70% of median box-entry times without shifts and 40% for a union over 16 shift choices. Extensions cover multiplayer games through cooperative comparison systems and explicit boxes, and discrete-time exponential-weights learning under explicit step-size conditions.
papers.summary: For finite bimatrix games, we give a payoff-based sufficient condition $E>0$ for an interior initial state to converge to a specified strict pure Nash equilibrium under replicator dynamics.

papers.title: Leverage-Enhanced Sampling Owen Method for Explainable Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.
papers.summary: Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability.

papers.title: Pure-Strategy Equilibrium in the Generalized First-Price Auction
papers.abstract: We revisit the classic result on the (non-)existence of pure-strategy Nash equilibria in the generalized first-price auction for sponsored search advertising and show that the conclusion may be reversed when ads are ranked based on the product of stochastic quality scores and bid amounts rather than solely on the bids or on the product of bids and deterministic quality scores. Moreover, the expected revenue in the pure-strategy equilibrium of the generalized first-price auction may substantially exceed that of the generalized second-price auction, although under some conditions, the relation may also be reversed. History: This paper has been accepted for the Mathematics of Operations Research Special Issue on Market Design.
papers.summary: We revisit the classic result on the (non-)existence of pure-strategy Nash equilibria in the generalized first-price auction for sponsored search advertising and show that the conclusion may be reversed when ads are ranked based on the product of stochastic…

papers.title: An Odd Approximation of Inflation for State Dependent Pricing Models
papers.abstract: We derive an aggregate state-space representation of state-dependent pricing models with random menu costs and strategic complementarities. The representation, derived from first principles, replaces the cross-sectional distribution of price gaps with a finite set of its moments (the first three), while preserving the key economic forces of state-dependent pricing--movements in the frequency of price adjustment and selection. Along the impulse response, inflation is an odd (cubic) polynomial in the average price gap. Embedded in a general equilibrium setting, the model can be solved by perturbation, filtered, and estimated with standard DSGE tools, and it matches well the global solution across shock sizes. Applied to the 2021--22 inflation surge in the United States and the euro area, it shows that much of the variation that linear models would attribute to cost-push shocks is in fact endogenous amplification through the frequency of price changes and selection.
papers.summary: We derive an aggregate state-space representation of state-dependent pricing models with random menu costs and strategic complementarities.

papers.title: Aging and Structural Change: Cost Disease in the Care Sector
papers.abstract: For most of the service sector, market productivity growth has pulled production out of the home. We show that formal nursing care is an exception because its productivity growth has been negative. A two-sector general equilibrium overlapping generations model with informal care attributes the rise in formal care's relative price to this decline, not demography. Care/non-care complementarity dominates formal/informal complementarity. As formal prices rise, elders substitute non-care consumption for formal care, shifting care onto informal caregivers. Population aging need not slow growth if non-care productivity rises or entering cohorts grow and its effects are offset by declining care needs.
papers.summary: For most of the service sector, market productivity growth has pulled production out of the home. We show that formal nursing care is an exception because its productivity growth has been negative.

papers.title: Paying Creators for Training Data Can Increase AI Displacement
papers.abstract: Generative AI increasingly competes with creators while using their content as training data. In response, policymakers have called for platforms to compensate creators for training data use and allow opting out. We study how such policies affect creator displacement in a model of a platform where creators choose whether to contribute training data and consumers choose between purchasing from creators and prompting generative AI trained on their content. When compensation is required, the low-quality creator chooses to remain solely as a training data supplier while AI fully displaces her demand, despite AI quality and the price the platform charges for AI-generated content being identical with and without compensation. Without compensation, the risk of losing creators and their training data constrains the platform to set the price of creators' content to preserve their demand. This constraint also prevents further AI displacement as AI improves, with the platform raising AI prices while keeping creators' prices and demand unchanged to prevent exit. Compensation increases creators' payoffs and total surplus but reduces consumer surplus. Our findings highlight how compensation policies for training data can shape creators' economic roles in a future with more capable generative AI.
papers.summary: Generative AI increasingly competes with creators while using their content as training data. In response, policymakers have called for platforms to compensate creators for training data use and allow opting out.

papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Welfare: Evaluating AI Buyers under Strategic Price Complexity in a Synthetic Duopoly
papers.abstract: AI buying agents may alter sellers' incentives as well as consumers' decisions. In a synthetic duopoly, we evaluate price-comparison pipelines on a fixed menu and in empirical correlated-equilibrium games. Calculator assistance selects an optimal offer 84.00% of the time, versus 68.57% under verified-total disclosure, yet disclosure has a 20.14-unit higher consumer-worst equilibrium surplus. A frozen-strategy holdout comparison favors disclosure, while re-solving equilibria under scenario resampling produces a range spanning zero. These model-based results show why accuracy, loss severity, seller incentives, and welfare incidence require separate measurement.
papers.summary: AI buying agents may alter sellers' incentives as well as consumers' decisions. In a synthetic duopoly, we evaluate price-comparison pipelines on a fixed menu and in empirical correlated-equilibrium games.

papers.title: The Rebundling of Freelance Work in the AI Age
papers.abstract: This paper examines how freelance work is changing in the AI era. We compare the activities people undertake in ChatGPT with the work clients request on Upwork, an online freelance platform, and examine how clients combine tasks into projects. We find that activities more prevalent in ChatGPT tend to lose marketplace share on Upwork, while those less prevalent tend to gain share. Within AI-related work, demand is becoming more diverse, and job postings combine tasks that were rarely requested together before the generative AI era. AI-related postings also have substantially larger project budgets and involve more hours of work, while differences in hourly rates are small. Together, these findings suggest that AI is reshaping not only which tasks clients outsource, but also how they combine tasks into larger, higher-value projects.
papers.summary: This paper examines how freelance work is changing in the AI era. We compare the activities people undertake in ChatGPT with the work clients request on Upwork, an online freelance platform, and examine how clients combine tasks into projects.

papers.title: Designing Information in a Forest: Algorithmic Aspects
papers.abstract: The Bayesian persuasion framework models strategic information revelation by a sender to one or more receivers. We study an intricate version of the multi-receiver persuasion setting in which the communication hierarchy is a forest - i.e., some receivers observe more informative signals than others, and the partial ordering of the receivers according to the information they get is represented by a pre-specified directed forest. This model naturally captures interactions in hierarchical organizations, and it lies in between the two most commonly studied versions of Bayesian persuasion: private persuasion and public persuasion. Inspired by the classic model of private persuasion, we focus on a setting with a binary state of nature and binary-action heterogeneous receivers s.t. the sender's utility is a monotone function of the set of receivers taking a specific desirable action. We extend the computational tractability result for symmetric sender's utility from private persuasion to the forest hierarchy framework using methodology inspired by optimal transport theory. We further provide a polynomial-time algorithm when the sender's utility is modular. On the negative side, we show that, unlike in private persuasion, the case of a supermodular sender's utility function leads to an NP-hard optimization problem which further does not admit an FPTAS unless P=NP; this result holds even when each tree component of the forest is a chain of 3 receivers. To complement the hardness result, we provide a simple approximation algorithm with the approximation ratio depending linearly on the depth of the forest hierarchy. We further provide an analogous algorithm for the submodular utility case. Finally, beyond forest communication hierarchies, we rule out an FPTAS for the sender's optimal utility even in the symmetric utility case, unless P=NP.
papers.summary: The Bayesian persuasion framework models strategic information revelation by a sender to one or more receivers.

papers.title: The Price of Anarchy in Markets for Lemons
papers.abstract: We study the worst-case equilibrium gains from trade in simple bilateral trade mechanisms with interdependent valuations. Equilibria in such settings are typically complex, as proposed prices can convey private information held by the proposer. Such equilibria suffer lost gains from trade both due to the inefficiency introduced by screening (as in independent private value settings) and due to adverse selection. We identify broad conditions under which, nevertheless, sequential equilibria are guaranteed to achieve a constant fraction of the first-best gains from trade. Our bounds quantify the central role of rare pessimistic seller signals and rare optimistic buyer signals. The results apply to seller-proposer, buyer-proposer, and random-proposer mechanisms. The key idea in our analysis is to relate equilibrium gains from trade to proposer profits in an auxiliary market with independent private values.
papers.summary: We study the worst-case equilibrium gains from trade in simple bilateral trade mechanisms with interdependent valuations. Equilibria in such settings are typically complex, as proposed prices can convey private information held by the proposer.

papers.title: When Better Artificial Intelligence Widens the Adoption Gap in Health Care
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can assist healthcare providers in clinical practice or replace services for which they are paid. We model how provider influence shapes two policy choices. The first is adoption, the share of cases in which coverage is switched to care using AI. The second is the review requirement, the number of paid reviews that must accompany AI when it is used in clinical care. Assistance can lower providers' costs and increase their profits while leaving paid reviews unaffected. However, increasingly capable AI may support autonomous use that can replace reviews and reduce providers' profits. Provider gains from adoption first rise and subsequently fall as AI capability improves. Hence, providers oppose sufficiently autonomous AI if their lost income from reviews exceeds savings from better assistance. Opposition to AI adoption arises earlier for AI that displaces more reviews. When providers can influence adoption but not the review requirement, their opposition causes under-adoption. The patient value forgone at the margin grows as AI improves. At interior policies, provider influence over both decisions widens adoption and raises review requirements above the patient optimum.
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) can assist healthcare providers in clinical practice or replace services for which they are paid. We model how provider influence shapes two policy choices.

papers.title: Knowing Less After a Diagnostic Test: Dilation in Clinical Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Dilation (Seidenfeld and Wasserman 1993) occurs when conditioning on new information \textit{only} increases uncertainty regardless of what the information reveals. Often viewed as an undesirable feature of models of ambiguity, dilation has sparked sustained debate about belief updating. This paper shows that following established clinical guidance can induce dilation, even for diagnostic tests that meet conventional performance benchmarks. We characterize when a test is dilation-inducing and show that a ubiquitous feature of performance studies -- evaluating tests against an imperfect reference -- creates scope for dilation. To facilitate detection before clinical use and inform regulatory standards, we develop a finite-sample valid hypothesis test of the null that a diagnostic test is dilation-inducing in this context. Applying the method to an influential study that preceded and contributed to the clinical adoption of chest CT screening for COVID-19, we find that the data are consistent with dilation.
papers.summary: Dilation (Seidenfeld and Wasserman 1993) occurs when conditioning on new information \textit{only} increases uncertainty regardless of what the information reveals.

papers.title: Who Observes Whom: Network Rationalizability and Its Complexity
papers.abstract: Nash equilibrium and rationalizability sit at opposite informational extremes: the former presumes that each player knows all opponents' strategies, the latter that players reason from common knowledge of rationality alone. When visibility is partial and asymmetric, we study the solution concepts induced by a directed \emph{observation network} $G$ in which an edge $i\to j$ means that $i$ observes $j$'s strategy. A set of profiles is \emph{self-sustaining} if every profile in it can be justified, for every player, by conjectures from the same set that agree with everything the player observes. We consider \emph{point} conjectures (single profiles) and \emph{belief} conjectures (distributions over profiles). Both range from Nash equilibrium on the complete network to point- and correlated rationalizability on the empty network, and shrink monotonically as links are added. Network topology governs both behavior and complexity. A predicted profile can be found in polynomial time on the empty network, whereas a single link makes search $\mathsf{PPAD}$-hard: under one-sided two-player monitoring, the observed player's strategies are exactly her Nash equilibrium strategies. On hierarchical networks (transitive tournaments), membership reduces recursively to smaller games and admits polynomial-size certificates, placing verification in $\exists\mathbb{R}$, and in $\mathsf{P}$ for two players. On the directed three-cycle, however, iterated elimination may never terminate under either variant, and under point conjectures interior predictions may admit only infinite witness sets, a pathology that belief conjectures avoid in the same game. Finally, when only realized pure actions are observed, the solution set is guaranteed to be non-empty exactly when the network has no edges, and is computable in time $O(n|A|^2)$.
papers.summary: Nash equilibrium and rationalizability sit at opposite informational extremes: the former presumes that each player knows all opponents' strategies, the latter that players reason from common knowledge of rationality alone.

papers.title: Disenfranchisement in Spatial Voting Games
papers.abstract: The questions of voting rights, group membership, and the boundaries of acceptable discourse all involve a recursive, self-stability issue, wherein the voters, group members, and acceptable commentators are often the ultimate arbiters of their own rules for inclusion and exclusion. In order to understand how ideological or issue diversity may impact the stability of such inclusion and exclusion, we introduce franchise elections, where voting members of a group vote to change the electorate. In particular, when agents are positioned inside an ideological or issue space, a social choice function that aggregates agent viewpoints induces a preference for agents over group composition, where agents prefer groups that improve the social choice function outcome for them. We demonstrate that when ideological space is two-dimensional, these franchise elections can generate complex behavior and that this complexity exists for any social choice function. Using the Yolk social choice function from voting theory, we illustrate that franchise elections can predict that agents attempting to introduce a new ideological axis perpendicular to an existing left-right spectrum risk disenfranchisement unless they ally with either side of the spectrum, and that franchise elections can cycle with any period.
papers.summary: The questions of voting rights, group membership, and the boundaries of acceptable discourse all involve a recursive, self-stability issue, wherein the voters, group members, and acceptable commentators are often the ultimate arbiters of their own rules for inclusion and exclusion.

papers.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
papers.abstract: Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity 1–5 . We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells) 6 . Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1 ) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 ( Rgs2 ), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.
papers.summary: Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity 1–5 .

papers.title: The sound of persuasion: Using generative AI to identify gender gaps in political influence
papers.abstract: Women often experience a deficit in persuasive influence, particularly in contexts like politics, where expectations about women’s behavior may conflict with gendered expectations about the domain and role. In spite of this widespread pattern, the mechanisms behind the gender gap in persuasion are difficult to isolate and test in dynamic political conversations. Women may be less persuasive simply because role-based expectations prompt others to afford women less authority when speaking about politics generally or about some political topics. Alternatively, women may be less persuasive because they tend to use linguistic patterns or rhetorical strategies that are less effective. Using an original AI-based approach, we put 4,300 human subjects into realistic, real-time phone conversations with an AI agent. These agents were randomly assigned either a masculine or feminine gendered conversation topic and a male- or female-sounding voice, allowing us to manipulate topic and perceptions of speakers’ gender while holding constant other elements of rhetorical content and strategy. After validating the experimental treatments, we find no direct effects of perceived gender of the AI agent, as cued by voice. However, gender affects other important aspects of the persuasive interaction. Research subjects were more likely to be persuaded about the masculine topic (defense spending) than the feminine topic (aid to the poor). Additionally, women research subjects were, on average, more persuaded than men. To the extent that men and women emphasize different topics in political conversations and have different discussion partners, these dynamics are likely to shape women’s political persuasive influence.
papers.summary: Women often experience a deficit in persuasive influence, particularly in contexts like politics, where expectations about women’s behavior may conflict with gendered expectations about the domain and role.

papers.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Constant-Factor EFX Allocations of Chores
papers.abstract: We study the fair division of indivisible chores among agents with additive disutilities, focusing on the central fairness notion of envy-freeness up to any chore (EFX), and its multiplicative approximations. Although the existence of constant-factor approximations to EFX are known, computing such an allocation in polynomial time remained open. We resolve this question by giving an algorithm that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, computes a $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX allocation in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$. Our result relies on two algorithmic contributions. First, we give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for earning-restricted (ER) equilibria with equal earning requirements and arbitrary feasible chore earning limits. We develop a new nonconvex program with chore payouts and money-flow variables, and prove that every local maximum yields an exact ER equilibrium. We then give a mirror-ascent algorithm for this program and prove that it converges to an approximate ER equilibrium in polynomial time. Second, we give a new procedure that converts the approximate equilibrium into a $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX-friendly allocation, a suitable starting point for the chore-swap framework of Garg and Murhekar (2026). The procedure uses a flexible price threshold to choose swap chores and their recipients together, overcoming a factor-four bottleneck in the earlier approaches while accommodating approximate earnings. We expect these ideas to be useful more broadly in fair division, including for goods and other fairness notions.
papers.summary: We study the fair division of indivisible chores among agents with additive disutilities, focusing on the central fairness notion of envy-freeness up to any chore (EFX), and its multiplicative approximations.

papers.title: Stochastic Games with Distributional Entropy Objectives
papers.abstract: We introduce \emph{stochastic games with distributional entropy objectives}, two-player zero-sum games whose configurations are probability distributions over the states of a finite arena and whose stage reward is Shannon entropy. Over an infinite discounted horizon, MIN seeks to concentrate the distribution, while MAX seeks to disperse it. Because entropy is nonlinear, it matters whether strategic and transition randomness are averaged before entropy is evaluated or sampled first. We formalise three resulting semantics: averaged-distribution, sampled-profile, and sampled-transition. This semantic choice fundamentally changes the game-theoretic structure. Averaged-distribution games need not be determined, even on a four-state deterministic arena, whereas both sampled semantics are determined and admit optimal stationary randomised strategies. We give contractive Bellman characterisations and convergent finite-horizon approximations for the upper and lower averaged values and the two sampled values. Moreover, even the lower value under averaged-distribution semantics dominates the value under either sampled semantics, while the sampled-profile and sampled-transition values are incomparable in general. For fixed rational discount and positive rational promise gap, the averaged-distribution (upper and lower value) gap problems and both sampled gap problems lie in PSPACE; for a single entropy minimiser, the averaged and sampled-profile problems lie in NP. Finally, under all three semantics, entropy optimisation is NP-hard to approximate within a suitable fixed additive constant, already for deterministic one-player games, where pure memoryless strategies are optimal.
papers.summary: We introduce \emph{stochastic games with distributional entropy objectives}, two-player zero-sum games whose configurations are probability distributions over the states of a finite arena and whose stage reward is Shannon entropy.

papers.title: Go under Chinese Rules with a Succinct Game History is Complete for Exponential Space
papers.abstract: The complexity of games is a central topic in combinatorics, algorithms, and computational complexity theory. It asks how difficult it is to determine the winner of a combinatorial game under optimal play. Many games, such as Hex or Othello, are PSPACE-complete: the game tree has polynomial depth, so the game can be decided in PSPACE. However, some games allow exponentially long plays, for instance Chess (without a generalized 50-move rule) or Go under Japanese rules; these are complete for exponential time. To prevent infinite games, some games employ a no-repetition rule (super-ko rule), for instance Go under Chinese rules. Robson (1984) proved that Chess and Checkers with a no-repetition rule are even harder: deciding whether the first player has a winning strategy is EXPSPACE-complete. Since then, it has been an open problem whether Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete, too. The complexity of a game under a no-repetition rule is typically interpreted as follows: given a board position, decide whether the first player has a winning strategy such that no repetition occurs from that position on. We introduce the concept of a succinct game history: a Boolean circuit that, given a board position, outputs 1 if the position is in the game history and 0 otherwise. It serves as a "judge" that tells the players whether a move is illegal because it creates a repetition. We prove that deciding whether Black has a winning strategy in Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete when the game history is given succinctly. Moreover, the starting position in our hardness proof is reachable by legal gameplay, which has not always been the case in prior proofs.
papers.summary: The complexity of games is a central topic in combinatorics, algorithms, and computational complexity theory. It asks how difficult it is to determine the winner of a combinatorial game under optimal play.

papers.title: The Tournament Equilibrium Set Is PSPACE-Complete, Even under Hereditary Uniqueness
papers.abstract: The tournament equilibrium set (TEQ), proposed by Schwartz in 1990, is a classical voting rule based on pairwise majority comparisons. Its definition is recursive: an alternative is judged by the alternatives that beat it, called its dominators, and by which of those dominators TEQ itself selects. Deciding whether a given alternative belongs to TEQ was known to be NP-hard and to lie in PSPACE. We close this gap by proving that the problem is PSPACE-complete. To our knowledge, this is the first PSPACE-completeness result for membership in a tournament solution. The hardness persists even when every nonempty subtournament has a unique minimal retentive set, the property conjectured by Schwartz to hold for all tournaments. Moreover, every such subtournament in our hard instances contains an alternative with at most three dominators. We prove that a single alternative with at most four dominators suffices both to guarantee uniqueness and to find a TEQ winner in $O(N^2)$ time. Thus, on our hard instances, finding one winner is efficient even though recognizing a specified winner is PSPACE-complete. We also study how the complexity changes with the dominator bound. If every nonempty subtournament has an alternative with at most one dominator, the entire TEQ can be computed in quadratic time; allowing two dominators makes membership NP-hard. Under the same condition with four dominators, all $t$ winners can be computed in $O(2^t N^2)$ time, where $N$ is the number of alternatives.
papers.summary: The tournament equilibrium set (TEQ), proposed by Schwartz in 1990, is a classical voting rule based on pairwise majority comparisons.

papers.title: Coverage-Aware Routing with Approximate Equilibrium Guarantees for Location-Diversity Vehicular Crowdsensing
papers.abstract: Vehicular crowdsensing uses the sensors of everyday vehicles to monitor cities, but traffic concentrates on few roads, leaving much of the network unsensed. Location-diversity incentives pay vehicles more to travel where few others go, but our earlier mechanism sets how far each vehicle deviates without optimizing collective coverage in route selection. We add this step in two stages. First, a non-cooperative game with diversity-weighted rewards yields each vehicle's equilibrium deviation. Second, the platform recommends to each vehicle a feasible route whose deviation is within a tolerance of this value, chosen to improve coverage. The coverage gain is monotone submodular, so a greedy router with local search attains at least half of the optimal gain over generated candidates. If every active vehicle has a candidate within a tolerance that is small relative to the aggregate deviation, the recommended routes form an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium, with $\varepsilon$ first order in the tolerance, or second order under a stronger condition. On London and Monaco road networks, the router achieves 99.4% and 98.9% of the optimal reduction in the coverage penalty on small instances and exceeds closest-length selection by up to 27.9 points. Under heterogeneous costs, uniform deviation needs compensation averaging 42% of the budget to give every vehicle nonnegative utility; the equilibrium targets need almost none. They also yield more coverage per unit of added travel in most settings and up to 22.6 more points at small budgets, an advantage that depends on placement and reverses at large budgets, where detour limits bind.
papers.summary: Vehicular crowdsensing uses the sensors of everyday vehicles to monitor cities, but traffic concentrates on few roads, leaving much of the network unsensed.

papers.title: Second-Best Trade Is Half Efficient in Multidimensional Markets
papers.abstract: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. The guarantee is achieved by a mechanism satisfying Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, and strong budget balance, and is tight already in single-item bilateral trade. Types are independent across agents, while the coordinates of each agent's type may be arbitrarily correlated. Feasibility constraints may couple trades across items and agents. This extends the known tight one-half guarantee for single-item bilateral trade. Our proof develops a new application of the Cai--Devanur--Weinberg duality framework. We show that the objective of every feasible dual is at least half of the first best. Strong duality then yields the guarantee without characterizing an optimal mechanism or dual. The key observation is that every feasible dual induces continuous-time Markov chains that, when stopped by exponential clocks, recover true types as expectations of virtual types. The dual constraints control the rate at which these chains change the prior distributions. We establish our bound by combining this control with a coupling of the agents' clocks.
papers.summary: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints.

papers.title: From the firm- to the application-level: A new typology of AI use in organisations
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is applied in organisations in many different ways. However, the firm-level literature on AI lacks a conceptual framework able to describe that variety. Empirical studies typically examine one dimension of AI use at a time. This paper argues that the difficulty follows from the unit of analysis: a firm may hold many AI applications at once, each with its own novelty, sourcing mode, objective and technology type. These dimensions are defined at the level of the application rather than of the firm. We therefore propose shifting the unit of analysis from the firm to the individual AI application, and develop a typology combining these four conceptual dimensions. The new framework locates any application in a common space, and it points out in particular two types that the prevailing adoption-innovation distinction neglects: co-invention, novel uses of technology the firm did not develop, and internalisation, in-house building of AI that could have been bought instead. Documented use cases illustrate the framework, which is then used to discuss implications for firms strategies and the diffusion of AI in economic systems.
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence is applied in organisations in many different ways. However, the firm-level literature on AI lacks a conceptual framework able to describe that variety. Empirical studies typically examine one dimension of AI use at a time.

papers.title: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence
papers.abstract: Curiosity, the drive to close the gap between what one knows and what one wants to know, pulls consumers beyond their familiar content, sustains engagement, and breaks them out of the filter bubbles of repetitive, relevance-only recommendations. Despite its importance, curiosity is hardly incorporated into modern recommender systems for lack of a formal measure. The information-gap theory of curiosity provides no formal quantitative model that a recommender system can operate on, and existing proxy metrics do not accurately measure the curiosity that a recommended item evokes. To fill this research gap, we formalize the information-gap theory into five axioms of curiosity and construct the canonical formulation of a computational measure of the curiosity that a recommended item evokes in a consumer. We validate our curiosity measure through a survey-based study, in which it matches consumers' self-reported curiosity and outperforms alternative proxy metrics. We subsequently build a curiosity-aware recommender system that incorporates this measure into the utility function design, and we show through offline experiments on three real-world datasets that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale online controlled experiment at a major video-streaming platform in Asia, where we show that our method significantly increases click-through rate, video views, and time spent over the latest production system, leading to tangible economic impact for the company. Our method has since been deployed on the platform and remains in operation. Our findings establish consumer curiosity as a measurable and actionable objective for recommender systems, with important managerial implications for digital platforms to recommend what consumers wonder about.
papers.summary: Curiosity, the drive to close the gap between what one knows and what one wants to know, pulls consumers beyond their familiar content, sustains engagement, and breaks them out of the filter bubbles of repetitive, relevance-only recommendations.

papers.title: Optimal Regulation and Information Institutions with Hidden Network Equilibria
papers.abstract: Aggregate outcomes can conceal network configurations that expose households to uninsurable risk and require different public services. We study a regulator's joint choice of a corrective activity charge and an information institution in a two-population network game. Although aggregate behavior follows an exact stable law, distinct specialization equilibria require different targeted interventions. With purchased Gaussian monitoring, primitive conditions imply a discontinuous switch between strong regulation without purchased information and informed specialization. The regulator may alternatively obtain signed certification or elicit a privately known state through a report backed by committed random audits. We characterize the three institutions' optimized values and the cost thresholds at which credible disclosure replaces government monitoring. The institutional choice also changes optimal regulation: even when certification and truthful reporting reveal the same state, costly audits favor less specialization and a higher corrective charge. This ordering and monotonicity in audit costs hold under an explicit interiority condition without global concavity of the audit problem. The institutional comparison is solved in the benchmark without feedback from anticipated policy, while the policy switch and strict institutional rankings admit local persistence under additional regularity conditions. Results depend on enforceable verification, restrictions on data access, and an explicitly limited institutional menu.
papers.summary: Aggregate outcomes can conceal network configurations that expose households to uninsurable risk and require different public services.

papers.title: Games Played by Exponential Weights Algorithms
papers.abstract: This paper studies the last-iterate convergence properties of the exponential weights algorithm with constant learning rates. We consider a repeated interaction in discrete time, where each player uses an exponential weights algorithm characterized by an initial mixed action and a fixed learning rate so that the mixed action profile [Formula: see text] played at stage t follows an homogeneous Markov chain. At first, we show that the probability to play a strict Nash equilibrium at the next stage converges almost surely to zero or one. Second, we show that the limit of [Formula: see text], whenever it exists, belongs to the set of Nash equilibria with equalizing payoffs. Finally, we show that in strong coordination games, where the payoff of a player is positive on the diagonal and zero elsewhere, [Formula: see text] converges almost surely to one of the strict Nash equilibria. Funding: This research benefited from financial support from the AI Institute Artificial and Natural Intelligence Toulouse Institute (ANITI) [Grants ANR-19-PI3A-0004 and ANR-23-IACL-P0002] and the ANR Chess [Grant ANR-17-EURE-0010]. J. Renault acknowledges funding from the Agence nationale de la recherche (ANR) [Grant MaSDOL-19-CE23-0017-01].
papers.summary: This paper studies the last-iterate convergence properties of the exponential weights algorithm with constant learning rates.

papers.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
papers.abstract: Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1–3. Recent advances in single-cell technologies have underscored the presence of intratumour heterogeneity, which poses substantial challenges in cancer treatment and achieving long-term disease-free survival4–7. Here we extensively profile epigenetic heterogeneity in a cohort of treatment-naive human luminal tumours, which were obtained directly after surgical resection. By applying a single-cell epigenetic approach based on cytometry by time-of-flight, we identify a recurrent subpopulation of basal-like cells in luminal tumours with a conserved epigenetic signature across patients. These basal-like cells, also identified by deconvolution of whole-genome DNA methylation patterns, are characterized by high expression of aggressive oncogenic traits and downregulation of hormone receptor signalling. Direct comparison of single-cell proteomic and genomic profiling of monomethylation and trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 revealed that these marks are key features associated with loss of luminal identity. Finally, we highlight the potential of concomitant single-molecule profiling of histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in blood as an epigenetic liquid biopsy approach for early diagnosis of breast cancer. Moreover, the epigenetic basal signature measured in blood is linked to prognosis, which enables the identification of patients at increased risk for disease relapse. Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.
papers.summary: Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1–3.

papers.title: Physiologic and pharmacologic role of the glucocorticoid receptor in germinal center B cells and plasmacytic differentiation
papers.abstract: In diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a malignancy derived from germinal center (GC) B cells, somatic hypermutation aberrantly targets glucocorticoid receptor (GR) binding sequences in the super-enhancer (SE) of multiple oncogenes. These events abrogate GR binding and deregulate the expression of the SE-linked gene, suggesting an important role of GR in normal and transformed GC B cells. Using a GC-specific Nr3c1 knockout mouse model and multi-omics analyses in murine and human GC B cells, here we show that, under physiological conditions, GR constitutively localizes to the nucleus, where it transcriptionally modulates signaling pathways implicated in GC homeostasis and plasmablast differentiation in part by antagonizing the repressive function of BCL6 on the plasma cell master regulators IRF4 and PRDM1. While loss of baseline GR activity led to mild GC hyperplasia and impaired plasmacytic differentiation, pharmacologic doses of glucocorticoids, a key component of DLBCL chemo-immunotherapy, were preferentially toxic to GC in a GC B cell–autonomous manner. These findings uncover a physiological role for GR in the GC reaction as well as in promoting plasmablast/plasma cell formation and provide insights into the specific activity of glucocorticoids in the treatment of DLBCL.
papers.summary: In diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a malignancy derived from germinal center (GC) B cells, somatic hypermutation aberrantly targets glucocorticoid receptor (GR) binding sequences in the super-enhancer (SE) of multiple oncogenes.

papers.title: Bouton-specific diversity of glutamate release from single parallel fiber axons in the cerebellum
papers.abstract: Sensorimotor processing relies on high-frequency signaling across widespread neuronal networks, during which synapses undergo rapid short-term plasticity (STP) that transiently enhances or depresses synaptic strength. Although STP is known to vary across cell types and postsynaptic targets, it remains unclear whether and how it is regulated at the level of individual synaptic boutons along the same axon. Here, we used two-photon imaging of a fast genetically encoded glutamate sensor expressed in cerebellar granule cells to monitor glutamate release from individual parallel fiber boutons during trains of activity. We showed that along single axons, glutamate transients were detected at nearly all boutons, and displayed a high diversity of STP profiles. At individual boutons, initial synaptic weight and STP were regulated separately. Synaptic weight was primarily driven by release probability ( P r ) and the apparent number of functional release sites ( N ), whereas STP was mainly supported by rapid mobilization of synaptic vesicles. At the molecular level, we show that Synapsin II contributes to bouton-specific heterogeneity in release properties. These findings reveal that STP is regulated at the level of individual boutons by specific molecular determinants, enabling fine-tuned control of information flow in cerebellar circuits. A single granule cell could therefore translate an identical presynaptic spike pattern into distinct release dynamics at each of its boutons, thus diversifying the temporal structure of the information delivered to Purkinje cells.
papers.summary: Sensorimotor processing relies on high-frequency signaling across widespread neuronal networks, during which synapses undergo rapid short-term plasticity (STP) that transiently enhances or depresses synaptic strength.

papers.title: The p38α MAPK–MK2 axis drives chemotherapy-mediated nuclear actin remodeling to promote ovarian cancer progression
papers.abstract: Nuclear F-actin facilitates DNA damage repair and contributes to cancer chemoresistance. However, the regulatory mechanisms controlling its dynamic polymerization in response to genotoxic stress remain poorly defined. A major barrier in nuclear actin research is the lack of tools for precise, high-throughput analysis. To systematically investigate nuclear F-actin assembly in DNA damage response, we developed a deep learning pipeline, named nFANet, for high-throughput detection and analysis of nuclear F-actin. Here, using ovarian cancer—a malignancy where chemoresistance is a major clinical obstacle—as a model, we showed that platinum-based chemotherapy robustly induces nuclear F-actin assembly. A subsequent kinome screening, in combination with the application of nFANet, identified the kinase p38α MAPK as a critical upstream regulator of platinum-induced nuclear F-actin assembly. Mechanistically, the p38α MAPK–MK2 signaling pathway promotes formin-mediated nuclear F-actin assembly in response to chemotherapy.
