papers.title: Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?
Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
papers.abstract: Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase 1,2 . Failure to efficiently restart and/or protect stalled replication forks is a major source of genomic instability 3–6 . Stalled forks can be restarted by a variety of mechanisms, including repriming downstream of the impediment 4 . In human cells, the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL promotes fork progression during replication stress 7–10 , but how its activity is coordinated by the replisome is unresolved. Here, by reconstituting replication fork stalling and restart with purified human proteins, we show that the CMG helicase directs PRIMPOL for efficient replication fork restart. Unexpectedly, the interaction between PRIMPOL and replication protein A 9,11 is not critical for fork restart in this system. We show that PRIMPOL binds directly to CMG, and a cryo-electron microscopy structure illustrates how this targets PRIMPOL specifically for leading-strand priming to minimize the size of post-replicative gaps. Ablating the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction abolishes fork restart in vitro and PRIMPOL-dependent DNA damage tolerance in human cells. Our work establishes PRIMPOL as an integrated component of the human replisome dedicated to leading-strand priming.
papers.summary: Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase 1,2 .

papers.title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores
papers.abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulates molecular traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm 1,2 . Its permeability barrier is formed by intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine-rich nucleoporins (FG-NUPs), whose physical state has long been debated 3–13 . Deciphering how FG-NUPs behave inside living cells is crucial for understanding how NPCs achieve both selective and rapid transport. By combining site-specific labelling with time-resolved fluorescence anisotropy, here we show that FG domains exhibit nanosecond-scale, liquid-like segmental motion in live cells, whereas reconstituted FG condensates undergo a liquid-to-solid transition in vitro. Experiments and molecular-dynamics simulations further show that importin-β, a principal nuclear transport receptor, and O-linked β- N -acetylglucosamine, a key post-translational modification of FG-NUPs, together stabilize the dynamic FG network. Finely balanced FG–FG and FG–importin-β interactions maintain FG-NUP liquidity and generate a radial organization in which importin-β is enriched near the NPC periphery and extended FG domains remain in the central channel, forming the transport barrier. This organization explains recent MINFLUX observations 14 of rim-biased transport trajectories and is supported here by direct MINFLUX imaging of importin-β in mammalian cells. Together, our results reconcile conflicting models of FG-NUP organization 4,5,7,9,15 and establish a framework for understanding how cellular context tunes intrinsically disordered proteins in health and disease.
papers.summary: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulates molecular traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm 1,2 . Its permeability barrier is formed by intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine-rich nucleoporins (FG-NUPs), whose physical state has long been debated 3–13 .

papers.title: AI wearables could exploit people’s most vulnerable moments
NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
papers.abstract: Disconnects between in vitro and in vivo results in experimental biology have long been recognized as potential hurdles to understanding health and disease. A prototypical example of such a disconnect is the NLRP3 inflammasome, which mediates inflammation in diverse settings of disease and protective immunity1,2. Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro requires two signals: (1) priming by pathogen-associated molecular patterns such as bacterial lipopolysaccharides and (2) activation by molecules that disrupt cellular homeostasis1,3. By contrast, the NLRP3 inflammasome in vivo is activated by lipopolysaccharide alone. The mechanisms that underlie the difference between in vitro and in vivo activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome are undefined. Here we report that extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness is a determinant of NLRP3 activities and that in vitro systems using physiological ECM stiffness enable one-signal in vivo-like NLRP3 activities to occur in human and mouse phagocytes. Physiological ECM stiffness induced expression of the transcription factor NRF2, which was found to be necessary for one-signal NLRP3 activation. Mechanistically, we identify Panx1 as an NRF2-regulated gene that promotes NLRP3 activity. Macrophages derived from the stiff matrix of the bone—osteoclasts—had reduced NRF2 levels and impaired NLRP3 activity. Moreover, alveolar macrophages from patients with pulmonary fibrosis displayed reduced NRF2 activity. Finally, NRF2 was required for antitumour immunity induced by cancer vaccines consisting of NLRP3 agonistic adjuvants. These findings indicate that NRF2 may be a transcriptional checkpoint that controls NLRP3 inflammasome activity. The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.
papers.summary: Disconnects between in vitro and in vivo results in experimental biology have long been recognized as potential hurdles to understanding health and disease.

papers.title: The public trusts scientists with AI — more than it does anyone else
Students need AI-free spaces to learn core skills
Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
papers.abstract: The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource 1 . However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs 2,3 . Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.
papers.summary: The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource 1 .

papers.title: Novel gene therapy lets drug dampen brain cell activity, reducing seizures
papers.abstract: In first clinical result using “chemogenetic” strategy, a team in China treated three patients to control epilepsy
papers.summary: In first clinical result using “chemogenetic” strategy, a team in China treated three patients to control epilepsy

papers.title: Limited genomic predictability of complex trait evolution despite genotype-phenotype stability
papers.abstract: Whether genomic data can be used to effectively predict adaptation in natural populations is unknown. Here, we tested the efficacy of genomic prediction of complex trait evolution by monitoring genome-wide allele frequencies and pigmentation variation in genetically diverse populations of Drosophila melanogaster during evolution in both field mesocosms and a controlled, lab-based setting. At two points during trait evolution, we produced a high-powered, well-resolved genotype-phenotype map that exhibited marked stability across independent populations. Although we were able to use this map to correctly infer the direction of pigmentation evolution in both the lab and field settings, the particular loci responding to selection were largely unpredictable based on the direction of trait evolution itself. Our results hold implications for the promise, and limitations, of genomic prediction.
papers.summary: Whether genomic data can be used to effectively predict adaptation in natural populations is unknown.

papers.title: Building a cell engineering toolbox
papers.abstract: Biological diversity and deep learning are harnessed for discovery

papers.title: IFITM1-mediated restriction of henipavirus entry is associated with ephrinB2 reorganization and confinement in membrane nanodomains
papers.abstract: Nipah (NiV) and Hendra (HeV) viruses are prototype henipaviruses (HNV) within the family of Paramyxoviridae . They are highly pathogenic zoonotic paramyxoviruses that cause fatal encephalitis in humans, with case fatality rates of 40 to 70%. These viruses use the receptor-binding protein (G) to engage host receptors ephrinB2 and/or ephrinB3, while the fusion protein (F) drives membrane fusion leading to virus entry and cell–cell fusion. Interferon-inducible transmembrane (IFITM) proteins restrict the infection of many unrelated viruses at virus entry. We show that the knockdown of IFITM1 enhances HNV entry and cell–cell fusion in both human epithelial and endothelial cells, while overexpression of IFITM1 inhibits both. Using single-molecule localization microscopy, we observed that IFITM1 forms nanoclusters on the plasma membrane that are enlarged upon interferon stimulation. IFITM1 clusters spatially co-occur with GM1-enriched, raft-like membrane domains. EphrinB2, a lipid raft resident, organizes into larger and denser clusters when associated with IFITM1, suggesting a preferential partitioning into membrane domains organized and/or influenced by IFITM1. Using single-particle tracking, we further show that lateral diffusion of ephrinB2 on the plasma membrane is confined in the presence of IFITM1. This confinement is not reversed by amphotericin B, nor is IFITM1-mediated NiV restriction. Our data show spatial reorganization and confinement of ephrinB2 within membrane domains that may be organized and/or influenced by IFITM1. These changes may contribute to HNV restriction, potentially by increasing the energy barrier for virus-cell membrane fusion and reducing productive virus-receptor encounters.
papers.summary: Nipah (NiV) and Hendra (HeV) viruses are prototype henipaviruses (HNV) within the family of Paramyxoviridae . They are highly pathogenic zoonotic paramyxoviruses that cause fatal encephalitis in humans, with case fatality rates of 40 to 70%.

papers.title: Principles of use of tensile J-curve materials in antagonistic arrangements
papers.abstract: Natural ligaments are soft connective tissues that provide high stretchability for dexterous flexibility but switch to high stiffness to protect the musculoskeletal system from excessive deformation. These two functions cannot be independently tuned in conventional engineering materials with linear or hyperelasticity. Biological materials achieve this tailored behavior through a highly nonlinear tensile response characterized by a J-shaped curve, featuring an extended “toe region” of low force up to intermediate strains followed by an inflection, called the “heel region” which marks the onset of nonlinear stiffening. Here, we aim to study the characteristics of J-curves to establish principles for their use in robotic mechanisms. We define and measure the J-curve features responsible for protectiveness and mobility, describe the effective stiffness and the level of nonlinearity as a function of pre-stretch, and elucidate how the J-curve decouples flexibility from damage protection. Experimental measurements reveal the performance advantages of twisted and coiled elastomeric J-curve materials in engineered antagonistic arrangements and highlight their unique design space compared with linear elastic systems. Furthermore, we present a conceptual analysis of exploiting J-curve materials in energy-efficient running as an outlook toward their use in bioinspired robots.
papers.summary: Natural ligaments are soft connective tissues that provide high stretchability for dexterous flexibility but switch to high stiffness to protect the musculoskeletal system from excessive deformation.

papers.title: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 participates in the internalization of arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins
papers.abstract: Microsatellite repeat expansion of the 5′ GGGGCC 3′ sequence in the C9orf72 gene is the most common monogenic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) translated from the mutant allele can be detected in postmortem brains of afflicted individuals. The arginine containing peptides, poly proline-arginine (poly-PR) and poly glycine-arginine (poly-GR), are particularly noxious to cells. Both can undergo cell-to-cell transmission, but underlying mechanisms are not understood. We found rapid internalization and nucleolar localization of bath-applied hemagglutinin (HA) tagged poly-PR with twenty repeats (HA-PR 20 ) in cell lines and neurons. Small molecule and RNAi approaches implicated a temperature-dependent, fluid phase endocytosis mechanism for HA-PR 20 . We sought to identify DPR-related cell surface uptake factors using µMap high-resolution proximity labeling. DPR–iridium conjugates identified candidate cell-surface proteins which were interrogated in a secondary RNAi screen. Focusing on our strongest candidate, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 (CSPG4), we showed cellular uptake of HA-PR 20 is reduced by inhibition of glycosaminoglycan chain synthesis and knockdown or ablation of CSPG4. Knockdown of CSPG4 protected PR 20 -induced neuronal toxicity. Using a dual reporter system to interrogate in vitro neuron-to-neuron transmission of PR 50, we found PR 50 synthesized by one neuron readily spread to neighboring cells. Transmission was significantly reduced with CSPG4 knockdown. Similarly conditioned media from PR 50 or GR 50 expressing neurons contained transmissible protein that was internalized into neurons in a CSPG4-dependent manner. These results suggest CSPG4 participates in poly-PR/poly-GR internalization and transmission.
papers.summary: Microsatellite repeat expansion of the 5′ GGGGCC 3′ sequence in the C9orf72 gene is the most common monogenic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia.

papers.title: Transoceanic dispersals and island extinctions shape global snipe and woodcock diversity
papers.abstract: Island colonization through transoceanic dispersal has been central in shaping insular biodiversity. Following colonization, island populations often undergo morphological shifts, which may promote ecological specialization and endemism, but often increase vulnerability to extinction. Most species in the shorebird family Scolopacidae are highly migratory, which likely underpins their propensity for long-distance dispersal. Notably, snipes ( Gallinago , Coenocorypha ) and woodcocks ( Scolopax ) have colonized diverse island regions, including the southwest Pacific, Malay Archipelago, Japan’s Amami, and the Caribbean, although none of the extant island endemics are migratory. The southwest Pacific and Caribbean taxa have suffered substantial recent extinction driven by human impacts. Here, we investigate avian evolutionary and biogeographic dynamics using a combination of morphology and phylogenomic data from target capture sequencing of key extant and extinct snipes and woodcocks. Our results reveal four independent dispersals from the Eastern to Western Hemisphere and a trans-Pacific dispersal from South America to the southwest Pacific islands. Comparative analyses of migratory behavior and morphology demonstrate pronounced changes in insular groups. For example, the small Austral snipes Coenocorypha are nested within Gallinago , sister to a group of much larger, continental South American snipes. Another case is the extinct Scolopax brachycarpa of Hispaniola which osteologically more resembles Scolopax , but genetically belongs to Gallinago . Gallinago brachycarpa and other extinct Caribbean snipes may represent a radiation that is lost forever. Our findings shed light on the processes that generate and erase avian diversity on islands, highlighting the dynamic interplay of dispersal, adaptation to novel conditions, and risk for extinction.
papers.summary: Island colonization through transoceanic dispersal has been central in shaping insular biodiversity.

papers.title: RNA and proteins joined up at the origins of life: Persistence is the point
papers.abstract: What drove nucleic acids (NA) into functional associations with proteins (PR) at the origins of life? We reason from polymer physics and the Central Dogma that the fitness value of cooperating through a division of labor—NA for replication fidelity and PR for functional fitness—is much higher than for either polymer alone. Our model shows a Pareto Front, where NA and PR can bootstrap each other to achieve autocatalytic cooperativity toward biology.
papers.summary: What drove nucleic acids (NA) into functional associations with proteins (PR) at the origins of life?

papers.title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs
papers.abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub–grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert–vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub–grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity science with ecology, offering a pathway toward bottom-up ecosystem understanding.
papers.summary: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions.

papers.title: Multi-omics characterization of white matter free water reveals genetic and vascular determinants of neurological disorders
papers.abstract: White matter free water (FW-WM), quantified using diffusion MRI, reflects extracellular water content and microstructural alterations within water matter, but its genetic architecture and clinical relevance remain largely uncharted. We conducted a multi-omics study integrating 42,039 individuals from the UK Biobank and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohorts to characterize tract-specific FW-WM across genetic, phenotypic, and proteomic dimensions. Genome-wide association analyses identified 27 independent loci and prioritized 88 genes, which were enriched in the genomic functional elements of vascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytes. Notably, 20 loci (74%) were novel compared to conventional white matter metrics. Both genetic predisposition to higher FW-WM and imaging-derived FW-WM were associated with a spectrum of neurological disorders. Specifically, imaging-derived FW-WM showed strong associations with stroke (OR = 3.14) and dementia (OR = 4.15), while higher baseline FW-WM predicted progression from MCI to AD (HR = 2.58). Bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses further supported genetically predicted associations between hypertension and FW-WM, which were together associated with increased risks of stroke and cognitive impairment. Integrative proteomic analyses further nominated PEAR1 and ANGL3 as candidate proteins potentially linking hypertension-related vascular processes to FW-WM variation. Together, these findings provide a multi-omics characterization of FW-WM that connects genetic susceptibility, vascular factors, and neurological outcomes, supporting FW-WM as a tract-specific imaging phenotype with potential utility for neurological risk stratification.
papers.summary: White matter free water (FW-WM), quantified using diffusion MRI, reflects extracellular water content and microstructural alterations within water matter, but its genetic architecture and clinical relevance remain largely uncharted.

papers.title: Endosomal mRNA transport coordinates local mitochondrial bioenergetics during polar fungal growth
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial function relies on the precise spatial coordination of protein synthesis and import. Most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and must be supplied across varying intracellular distances. In highly polarized cells such as fungal hyphae and neurons, active long-distance mRNA transport is thought to sustain distal mitochondrial function, but its mechanistic coupling to protein import and organelle physiology is unclear. Here, we demonstrate that endosomal transport of mRNAs encoding mitochondrial proteins orchestrates local bioenergetics in infectious hyphae of Ustilago maydis . Using the subunit Atp3 of electron transport chain Complex V as a model, we uncover that the endosomal mRNA transporter Rrm4 is required for efficient mitochondrial protein import, particularly at growth poles. Loss of Rrm4 leads to defects in mitochondrial import, resulting in altered physiology. We propose that endosome-coupled mRNA transport constitutes a fundamental layer of subcellular mitochondrial homeostasis, with implications extending from fungal pathogenicity to neuronal disease.
papers.summary: Mitochondrial function relies on the precise spatial coordination of protein synthesis and import. Most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and must be supplied across varying intracellular distances.

papers.title: Evolution, information content, and optimality of gene regulatory architectures
papers.abstract: Evolution of genetic regulatory sequences is shaped by their genotype–phenotype map, but this map itself can evolve via changes in the molecular machinery that reads out the regulatory sequences. Using population genetics theory, we derive a maximization principle, which implies that genotype–phenotype maps will evolve to associate fit phenotypes with larger numbers of possible genotypes. Mathematically, this builds on analogies between population genetics and statistical physics, as well as optimal coding in information theory. The results are particularly interesting in the context of transcriptional regulation, where optimal values of certain parameters that determine the gene regulatory architecture can be derived even without a complete knowledge of the molecular mechanisms involved. We illustrate the theory using a simplified model of transcription factor (TF) binding to cis-regulatory elements (CREs): the fraction of possible CREs across the entire genotype space that bind a given TF evolves to match the fraction of CREs under selection to bind that TF. Similar “frequency matching” results are expected to emerge generically, because selection implicitly moves the entire regulatory architecture toward a fitness maximum, determining the “replicated genotype–phenotype map” for all CREs, while it simultaneously adapts toward individually fit CREs on that map. We discuss the subtleties and limitations of the theory related to biophysical constraints and the need for mutational robustness. Last, our theory suggests a possible mathematical definition for evolvability with predictive power that can be tested in evolutionary simulations and, ultimately, in comparative genetics studies.
papers.summary: Evolution of genetic regulatory sequences is shaped by their genotype–phenotype map, but this map itself can evolve via changes in the molecular machinery that reads out the regulatory sequences.

papers.title: Extracellular vesicles presenting “don’t eat me” signal limit the efferocytic capacity in lung fibrosis
papers.abstract: Efferocytosis is essential for tissue homeostasis and resolution of inflammation, yet its direct contribution to resolve organ fibrosis remains poorly understood. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive age-driven lung disease, we found profound suppression of efferocytosis coupled with robust production and release of extracellular vesicles presenting functional receptor CD47, a canonical “don’t eat me” mediator. Restoration of efferocytosis contributes to the natural resolution of fibrosis, which is accelerated by CD47 deficiency or alterations in macrophage metabolic responses. In turn, pharmacologic disruption of efferocytic receptors or signaling results in lung fibrosis development and its persistence. While sustained reduction of efferocytic capacity align with fibrosis persistence in aged mice, AMPK activation promotes fibrosis resolution via reducing inflammaging and CD47 bioavailability, thus restoring clearance of apoptotic fibroblast. Importantly, AMPK activation also reprograms macrophages engaging apoptotic fibroblasts toward a fibrosis pro-resolving phenotype by suppressing TGF-β1 and promoting secretion of pro-regenerative hepatocyte growth factor (HGF). Together, these findings link metabolism and immune efferocytic fitness in lung fibrosis resolution and suggest that an AMPK senomorphic pathway has broad therapeutic relevance for fibrotic diseases.
papers.summary: Efferocytosis is essential for tissue homeostasis and resolution of inflammation, yet its direct contribution to resolve organ fibrosis remains poorly understood.

papers.title: Competitive disruption of COI1 receptor assembly by a hemibiotrophic bacterial effector suppresses jasmonate-mediated immunity
papers.abstract: Hormone pathways are central hubs in plant immunity, and their receptors, the critical initiators of signaling cascades, are logical targets of pathogen effectors. The jasmonic acid (JA) pathway is a cornerstone of defense against phytopathogens, especially necrotrophs. However, whether pathogens can directly target its receptor COI1 to subvert this defense layer has remained unclear. Here, we show that JA signaling positively regulates resistance to the devastating hemibiotrophic pathogen Ralstonia solanacearum and identified a bacterial effector, RipBO, that directly targets COI1 to counteract this defense. RipBO binds with high affinity to the F-box domain of COI1, competitively disrupts the COI1-ASK interaction, and thereby blocks SCF COI1 complex assembly. This disruption effectively stabilizes JAZ repressors and paralyzes JA-mediated immunity. Our findings clarify the contribution of JA signaling to bacterial wilt resistance and identify direct targeting of the hormone receptor as a pathogen virulence strategy, pointing to a potential vulnerability for crop protection.
papers.summary: Hormone pathways are central hubs in plant immunity, and their receptors, the critical initiators of signaling cascades, are logical targets of pathogen effectors.

papers.title: The AI scientist in the mirror: Shared flaws, joint remedies
The Role of Parental Beliefs and Public Policies in Financing Higher Education: An Experimental Study
papers.abstract: Parents who want to financially support their child’s pursuit of higher education must save against assumptions about what college will cost and how it will be funded. This study examines how parental beliefs and future borrowing costs shape college saving decisions. Through a survey experiment with an embedded financial planning tool, we elicit parental beliefs about the future costs of college and their expectations of different funding sources, including financial aid and student loans. We find that nearly all parents want to cover some of the future costs of college, but many may fall short in their savings due to underestimating future expenses and overestimating available financial aid. A corrective information intervention encourages most parents to recalibrate their saving target. However, when a substantial gap between expected and actual costs is combined with a salient high repayment burden for their child, we find a discouragement effect that diminishes both their willingness to save and their aspirations for their child’s educational attainment. We calibrate a model of parental saving with learning about college costs, which reproduces both the absence of an average response to borrowing costs and the shift of children away from college attendance, and use it to price the welfare cost of misperception. Parents with higher financial literacy hold better-calibrated beliefs and respond more to correction. We discuss policy implications for outreach activities to support informed financial planning for college education.
papers.summary: Parents who want to financially support their child’s pursuit of higher education must save against assumptions about what college will cost and how it will be funded.

papers.title: Childhood Learning and Adult Earnings in Four LMIC Cohorts
papers.abstract: Researchers and policymakers in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) have customarily relied on indirect evidence to justify investments in learning, either by linking test scores to economic growth or by connecting adult cognitive assessments to earnings. This reliance on indirect evidence largely stems from the scarcity of longitudinal data linking school-age learning to adult earnings. We address this gap by using data from Ethiopia, India, Pakistan, and Peru to estimate associations between foundational learning (FL), measured by test scores around age 12, and human capital and earnings in young adulthood. In Peru, India, and Pakistan, a one-standard-deviation increase in FL is associated with an 8-13 log point increase in adult earnings. Childhood scores also predict 1.1-1.5 additional years of schooling and 9.3-13.5 percentage points higher college or vocational attendance, as well as higher skills in adulthood. Interestingly, a linear-projection decomposition indicates that measured schooling and adult test scores explain between 18% (Peru) to 50-56% (India and Pakistan) of the FL-earnings gradient, suggesting that FL may raise earnings over and above the association with schooling and adult scores. Finally, FL can account for about 5-12 percent of the earnings gap between young Ethiopians and Indians in our sample, a number that could rise to 33 percent as returns to learning grow over the life cycle. We interpret these descriptive findings in light of recent causal evidence on the learning-to-earnings pipeline and discuss the implications for policy investments in FL.
papers.summary: Researchers and policymakers in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) have customarily relied on indirect evidence to justify investments in learning, either by linking test scores to economic growth or by connecting adult cognitive assessments to earnings.

papers.title: Preconception Medicaid and Maternal and Infant Health: Evidence from Linked Administrative Data
papers.abstract: Despite pregnancy-focused public insurance coverage in the U.S., low-income mothers and infants face persistent health disadvantages. Using linked birth, tax, and enrollment data, we examine the effects of preconception coverage from California's 2014 Medicaid expansion, comparing changes in outcomes for first-time mothers just below and above the income eligibility threshold. Expansion increased preconception Medicaid enrollment by 3.4 months (+23 percentage points in 12-month continuous coverage), first-month pregnancy enrollment by 24 percentage points, and adequate prenatal care and STI screening. Yet we find no improvements in maternal or infant health, suggesting preconception coverage alone cannot close health disparities.
papers.summary: Despite pregnancy-focused public insurance coverage in the U.S., low-income mothers and infants face persistent health disadvantages.

papers.title: How Does Capital Flow To Poor Countries? Evidence from Venture Capital and Private Equity
papers.abstract: Why does so little private capital flow to poor countries? We study how venture capital and private equity investors evaluate firms across countries, using an experimental survey of 1,485 investors in 108 countries who are incentivized to evaluate hypothetical investment opportunities with randomized firm characteristics, locations, and investment terms. Investors respond similarly to firm fundamentals, but otherwise comparable firms attract substantially less interest in poorer countries. This poor-country penalty is much smaller among investors specialized in emerging markets. Detailed survey data show that emerging market and developed market investors have largely similar investment practices, but differ in how they obtain country information, assess and manage country risks, and exit investments. Investors reporting active country-risk management apply smaller country penalties, even after accounting for market focus. Our findings suggest that investors' specialization and investment practices shape how country risk affects investment: the same firm can face drastically different financing prospects depending on where it is located and which investors evaluate it.
papers.summary: Why does so little private capital flow to poor countries?

papers.title: Are Revealed Preferences All You Need for AI Alignment?
papers.abstract: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are. Cautious actions, such as deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks, and for choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block. Otherwise, the AI acts as its principal would yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions. Choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions miss.
papers.summary: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are.

papers.title: Aggregating Rankings of Coalitions to Rank Individuals
papers.abstract: We develop an ordinal framework for aggregating a profile of rankings of coalitional performances to determine the ranking of individuals. From university ratings to the assessment of team-sports players, we often evaluate individuals based on their coalitional performances. Although such evaluation has been addressed by cooperative game theory, it is only recently that its ordinal counterpart, social ranking theory (Moretti, 2015), has emerged. As most of the literature considers a single coalitional ranking (which corresponds to a real-valued characteristic function), we extend the model to allow a profile of coalitional rankings (which corresponds to a multidimensional characteristic function). We tackle the aggregation problem by introducing three families of inter-profile axioms, each representing how the rankings should interact or contribute to the output. After revealing fundamental impossibilities concerning the reconciliation of different families, we characterize a new solution, Pareto-extension Lex-cel (PEL), via some weaker versions of the inter-profile axioms. PEL extends Lex-cel, which is a central solution in social ranking theory, by analogy with Sen's Pareto extension rule. Our results develop the connection between classical Arrovian aggregation, cooperative game theory, and social ranking theory.
papers.summary: We develop an ordinal framework for aggregating a profile of rankings of coalitional performances to determine the ranking of individuals.

papers.title: Endogenous Parcel Contiguity and Rent Indeterminacy in a Finite-Household Monocentric City
papers.abstract: We study a monocentric city with finitely many households, each of which may hold any measurable set of land and incurs commuting costs that depend on the spatial distribution of its holdings. In equilibrium, every parcel is an interval and parcels are ordered by lot size from the center outward. The freedom to adjust land holdings at any location restricts supporting rents to a band between the competing bid rents and the assigned household's bid rent. This band excludes rents that support the same allocation when lots are restricted to intervals, including the one constructed by Berliant and Fujita (1992), and makes the existence of a supporting rent a substantive question even with identical households. We give sufficient conditions for the existence of a locally supporting rent that meets every household's budget and deters all small deviations. We also show that any equilibrium minimizes the real resource cost of attaining equilibrium utilities and extend the sorting result to heterogeneous households under a single-crossing condition. Finally, we discuss the relation to hedonic models, distinguishing the prices of whole parcels from location-specific rents that govern the cost of changes in parcel boundaries and fragmentation.
papers.summary: We study a monocentric city with finitely many households, each of which may hold any measurable set of land and incurs commuting costs that depend on the spatial distribution of its holdings.

papers.title: The Cherry-Picking Trap
papers.abstract: When a better-informed proposer puts forward a policy proposal, the responder should not take the proposal at face value but ask why it was chosen. We model how this inference can undermine trust even when interests are broadly aligned. A proposer privately observes a "basket" of viable policies and proposes one; a responder decides whether to approve the proposal but may lack the expertise to evaluate it. A larger basket makes a Pareto improvement more likely to be available but also gives the proposer greater scope to cherry-pick a policy that favors him at the responder's expense. In the unique equilibrium, Pareto improvements are often proposed and yet rationally rejected. Flexibility that should enable agreement instead breeds distrust.
papers.summary: When a better-informed proposer puts forward a policy proposal, the responder should not take the proposal at face value but ask why it was chosen. We model how this inference can undermine trust even when interests are broadly aligned.

papers.title: A Combinatorial Characterization of Immunity to the Strong Braess Paradox
papers.abstract: In a nonatomic congestion game, a strong Braess paradox occurs when reducing resource costs, population demands, or both increases at least one population's equilibrium cost. We characterize immunity when each population's available strategies form a fixed finite family of nonempty subsets of a common resource set. Immunity means that no such paradox can arise for any nonnegative continuous nondecreasing resource cost functions common to all populations and any positive demand vector. Our characterization resolves the open question posed by Fujishige et al.(2017) without varying the resource embedding. A menu is positively exposed if it consists of all available strategies of minimum total weight for some strictly positive resource weights. For a single population, we prove that immunity holds if and only if the column matroid of the augmented incidence matrix is series-parallel for every positively exposed menu. For multiple populations, we consider one menu for each population, all exposed by the same positive weights. The associated dual matroid includes one labeled element for each population to track its demand. Immunity holds if and only if, for every such collection of menus, each marked resource block is series-parallel and all demand labels retained in that block are parallel. We establish these characterizations through an affine response criterion and a blockwise ray lemma. Our results recover the immunity of matroid base systems under arbitrary resource sharing and the series-parallel routing criterion for complete acyclic path systems. Whenever a strategy system is not immune, we construct a strong Braess paradox with all demands equal to one and affine resource costs having strictly positive slopes and intercepts, by lowering just one intercept while keeping it positive. When strategies are listed explicitly, nonimmunity has polynomial-size certificates.
papers.summary: In a nonatomic congestion game, a strong Braess paradox occurs when reducing resource costs, population demands, or both increases at least one population's equilibrium cost.

papers.title: How to Defeat a Mafia (of Size 1)
papers.abstract: The game "Mafia'' is a social deduction game where $n$ players attempt to uncover a covert coalition of $m$ players among the $n$. Typically, $d=1$ of the non-coalition players are labelled ``Detective'' and have special abilities. Most game-theoretic analysis considers, however, only the variant without a Detective. Once the Detective role is introduced, extremely complex strategies can be employed, for which reason only upper and lower bounds for winning have been established, namely by considering specific strategies. We analyse the case $m=d=1$, providing a first example where an explicit, provably-optimal strategy can be described beyond $d=0$.
papers.summary: The game "Mafia'' is a social deduction game where $n$ players attempt to uncover a covert coalition of $m$ players among the $n$. Typically, $d=1$ of the non-coalition players are labelled ``Detective'' and have special abilities.

papers.title: Who Moved the Frontier? Paying Open Frontier Challenges with Free Identities
papers.abstract: In an open frontier challenge, anyone, person or AI agent, submits changes to a shared problem, and a change that beats the best measured score becomes the public baseline. How should it pay when identities are free? Rank prizes can be gamed: on a replay of one track of a recent challenge, one solver's steps under two identities would have taken first and second prize. We consider a prediction-market rule, proposed for machine-learning contests, that pays each accepted step for the progress it adds; with exact scores, among rules that see only a step's start and end, only these resist splitting and merging, and extra identities gain nothing. With noisy scores and independent normal runs, we prove that any payment that never takes money back and pays real improvements also pays something, on average, to a change that does nothing. We propose a fee per submission, at least what luck pays per attempt, that removes each attempt's expected profit if verifiers are honest and no submission is noisier than planned; nothing enforces that bound, and under noise the rule does not cap the total paid. If crediting another and faking credit to one's second account look the same, a rule that neither rewards fakes nor punishes honesty pays for credit at most what lying costs. We introduce a royalty on how much a later gain falls without the earlier change, which needs no claims but needs removable changes. For five public challenges, we name the rule our results would support.
papers.summary: In an open frontier challenge, anyone, person or AI agent, submits changes to a shared problem, and a change that beats the best measured score becomes the public baseline. How should it pay when identities are free?

papers.title: Artificial Currency and Separate Selling: A 3-Approximation for Consumer Surplus
papers.abstract: We study the allocation of indivisible items to buyers with additive values drawn from independent distributions. The objective is consumer surplus net of burnt payments. We consider artificial-currency mechanisms: buyers receive personalized budgets of a currency worthless outside the mechanism and use them to bid across items. The better of separate selling and artificial-currency mechanisms provides a 3-approximation to optimal consumer surplus. The guarantee holds at every Bayes--Nash equilibrium, without equilibrium selection. Both branches are necessary: either alone may capture only a vanishing share of the optimum. The proof decomposes benchmark surplus into a stable part captured by artificial currency and a variation covered by separate selling.
papers.summary: We study the allocation of indivisible items to buyers with additive values drawn from independent distributions. The objective is consumer surplus net of burnt payments.

papers.title: Trade Tensions Meet the Gig Economy: Evidence from the 2025 Halving of Chinese Travel to Japan
papers.abstract: How do geopolitical shocks to services exports reach local labor markets? Using China's November 2025 Japan travel advisory and postings on Japan's largest spot-work platform, we provide the first such evidence for the gig economy. Posted hourly wages fall immediately and persistently in prefectures more dependent on Chinese visitors, relative to others, whereas postings, hours, and employment show no robust change. Wages fall more for early morning and daytime shifts, when hotels and shops hire, than for evening and night shifts. Where each shift is priced anew, a services-trade shock lowers the price of labor in the hours it hits.
papers.summary: How do geopolitical shocks to services exports reach local labor markets? Using China's November 2025 Japan travel advisory and postings on Japan's largest spot-work platform, we provide the first such evidence for the gig economy.

papers.title: China's Local Government Debt, Strategic Competition, and Bitcoin Demand: A Conditional Transmission Framework
papers.abstract: How might the resolution of China's local-government debt affect strategic competition and Bitcoin demand? This paper develops a conditional framework connecting debt accounting, bank balance-sheet adjustment, public spending priorities, and constrained portfolio substitution. A debt swap can increase recognized government debt without increasing consolidated principal, while its effect on credit capacity depends on capital relief, loss recognition, and recapitalization. A protected strategic-spending floor can preserve current effort while shifting adjustment toward civilian productive services. In the asset block, stronger relative preference for Bitcoin does not ensure greater effective demand: access constraints and global funding conditions can reverse the sign. We derive a finite-shock threshold and deterministic sign bounds, and distinguish Bitcoin demand from demand for dollar stablecoins. Reproducible numerical illustrations and channel-removal exercises show that opposite outcomes are compatible with the same assumed fiscal stress. The analysis uses dated primary sources to establish institutional context, but estimates neither a debt-to-Bitcoin causal coefficient nor a price-impact scale. Its contribution is a compact set of conditions and measurement distinctions for evaluating transmission claims, rather than an unconditional price forecast or an inference about conflict probabilities.
papers.summary: How might the resolution of China's local-government debt affect strategic competition and Bitcoin demand?

papers.title: Huge If True: Learning from the Size of the Surprise
papers.abstract: Responses to earnings surprises depend on an unknown multiplier mapping earnings to value. Investors, however, learn about the news and the multiplier from the same number. Large surprises may indicate small multipliers and tiny surprises large ones. We model how greater uncertainty about the multiplier attenuates responses on average but makes them steeper near zero surprises. In an incentivized experiment, we find that greater processing constraints lower average sensitivity but raise it near zero. We confirm this with real-world earnings announcements: stocks with higher valuation uncertainty, our proxy for multiplier uncertainty, respond less on average but more steeply near zero.
papers.summary: Responses to earnings surprises depend on an unknown multiplier mapping earnings to value. Investors, however, learn about the news and the multiplier from the same number. Large surprises may indicate small multipliers and tiny surprises large ones.

papers.title: Economic Benefits of Cross-Border Electricity Trade and Domestic Electricity Production in Switzerland
papers.abstract: This paper assesses the economic benefits of cross-border electricity trade in the context of rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty. Switzerland provides a particularly compelling case because of its geographical location and limited integration into the EU electricity market. We first use the Nexus-e framework to simulate the generation capacity and transmission grid expansion required under autarky and free-trade scenarios. Based on these capacity configurations, a fundamental power market model simulates wholesale market outcomes under projected demand and generation conditions for 2040. By jointly accounting for consumer and producer surplus, as well as investments in generation capacity and grid infrastructure, we provide a comprehensive assessment of the welfare effects of cross-border electricity trade, leading to an estimated EUR 1.5 billion gain. More specifically, open access to cross-border electricity trade implies a EUR 1.8 billion transfer from largely publicly owned producers to consumers. Finally, we provide an illustrative, non-causal mapping of broader macroeconomic effects. Under a price-convergence assumption, the implied demand adjustment corresponds to a GDP-equivalent effect of approximately EUR 7 billion.
papers.summary: This paper assesses the economic benefits of cross-border electricity trade in the context of rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty.

papers.title: Uncovering internal sensory evidence reveals the nature of confidence computation in multi-alternative perceptual decision making.
papers.abstract: A central goal of perceptual decision making is to determine the computations underlying choice and confidence in complex, multi-alternative tasks. However, revealing these computations requires knowledge of the internal sensory evidence upon which the computations operate. Unfortunately, unlike for two-choice tasks, there is no established method in multi-alternative tasks to determine how stimuli are transformed into internal sensory evidence. Here we address this critical gap by developing a novel modeling paradigm that reveals how the brain transforms external stimuli into internal sensory evidence during multi-alternative decision making in the context of numerosity tasks. Across three experiments that feature two-, three-, and five-choice conditions, we show that the internal sensory evidence in our numerosity task can be described with a simple, two-parameter equation that fits data for up to 12 conditions. Critically, the ability to model the internal sensory evidence allowed us to test six theories of confidence computation. Our results support a model where confidence reflects the raw evidence difference between the top two alternatives. These results establish a new numerosity paradigm in which a two-parameter equation can be used to determine the internal sensory evidence for a potentially unlimited number of multi-alternative conditions and reveal the confidence computation in multi-alternative tasks.
papers.summary: A central goal of perceptual decision making is to determine the computations underlying choice and confidence in complex, multi-alternative tasks.

papers.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference
papers.abstract: When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships—not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants ( N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus ( N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference ( P < 0.001, Cohen’s d = −0.89, 95% confidence interval −1.41 to −0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.
papers.summary: When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships—not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge.

papers.title: Bellman Optimality of Average-Reward Robust Markov Decision Processes with a Constant Gain
papers.abstract: Learning and optimal control under robust Markov decision processes (MDPs) have received increasing attention, yet most existing theory, algorithms, and applications focus on finite-horizon or discounted models. Long-run average-reward formulations, while natural in many operations research and management contexts, remain underexplored. This is primarily because the dynamic programming foundations are technically challenging and only partially understood, with several fundamental questions remaining open. This paper steps toward a general framework for average-reward robust MDPs by analyzing the constant-gain setting. We study the average-reward robust control problem with possible information asymmetries between the controller and an S-rectangular adversary. Our analysis centers on the constant-gain robust Bellman equation, examining both the existence of solutions and their relationship to the optimal average reward. Specifically, we identify when solutions to the robust Bellman equation characterize the optimal average reward and stationary policies, and we provide one-sided weak communication conditions ensuring solutions' existence. These findings expand the dynamic programming theory for average-reward robust MDPs and lay a foundation for robust dynamic decision making under long-run average criteria in operational environments.
papers.summary: Learning and optimal control under robust Markov decision processes (MDPs) have received increasing attention, yet most existing theory, algorithms, and applications focus on finite-horizon or discounted models.

papers.title: Identifying Time Preference Shocks: Stated and Revealed Preferences after an Italian Earthquake
papers.abstract: Identifying time preference shocks is challenging: shocks large enough to shift survey-elicited stated impatience also tighten financial resources, confounding the interpretation of stated time preference. Jointly examining stated and revealed preferences resolves this identification problem: impatience shocks and reductions in financial resources generate opposite consumption responses, even though both raise stated impatience. Applying our identification framework to the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake, we combine panel data with spatially granular seismic and damage data in a difference-in-differences design that compares undamaged households that experienced the earthquake with a spatial control group at similar distances from the epicenter. Treated households report greater impatience and increase nondurable consumption by 11 percent relative to controls. Effects are consistent with a psychological stress channel, concentrated among the most vulnerable to stress, and persist as households deplete their liquid wealth buffer over time.
papers.summary: Identifying time preference shocks is challenging: shocks large enough to shift survey-elicited stated impatience also tighten financial resources, confounding the interpretation of stated time preference.
